scaffolding.title: What does roof scaffolding cost in New Zealand?
scaffolding.description: Compare scaffold price units, edge protection, setup and weekly hire with NZ supplier examples, clear scope limits and roof-access planning questions.
scaffolding.answer: Roof access prices depend on the system, height, perimeter, ground, working platforms and hire period. There is no single comparable “per-metre scaffold” price without those details. Full working scaffold and edge protection are different scopes, and scaffold elevation area is not roof area.

sections.title: What do NZ providers publish?

blocks.text: ScaffoldMe also reports a builder’s rental example: $4,000 setup/dismantle plus $190 per week, in the context of a 65 lm single-level package. The GST basis of that rental example is not explicit. It is not a current four-plank hire quotation.

We do not convert a three-plank supplier example into a verified four-plank rate. Upwell’s layout totals also differ from its headline rates and some example arithmetic is inconsistent. Confirm the actual quote; RoofHub does not copy those totals into the estimator.

sections.title: Is “per metre” length or area?

blocks.text: A lineal rate uses the measured run around the building. An elevation-area rate typically uses length × scaffold height, summed for the relevant faces. A roof-area rate is a third unit and cannot be substituted. Upwell explicitly describes the elevation-area approach.

For illustration only, a 60 m run at an assumed 3 m scaffold height is 180m² of elevation. At $18.50/m² setup and $1.50/m²/week, the arithmetic is $3,330 setup plus $270/week, excluding GST. It is not a four-plank quote, a design, or permission to assume that every single-storey building needs a 3 m scaffold.
That is also why simply multiplying a roof’s 200m² by a scaffolder’s m² rate can produce a wrong answer even though both numbers appear to use square metres.

sections.title: Can edge protection be used for a reroof?

blocks.text: Edge protection is a recognised risk-control approach, but it is not equivalent to a full working platform and it does not by itself address every roof-work hazard. A competent assessment must select suitable protection for the work and site.

RoofHub only offers the edge-protection planning option for eligible single-storey inputs. That is a product limitation, not a statement that NZ law bans it at two storeys. Selecting or excluding a cost estimate never waives the need for safe access.
WorkSafe’s older roof-work guide carries a notice about outdated legislation. We link it for the distinction between roof-edge and through-roof risks, not as a current compliance certificate.

sections.title: What does the RoofHub calculator assume?

blocks.text: Its working scaffold card separates one- and two-storey options, flat and difficult sites, and additional hire after four included weeks. Those ranges are project-planning allowances developed for this tool. They have not been converted into independently verified national tariffs.

A hillside can change the height, component quantities and work required. It may affect hire as well as setup, so the estimator’s simple rate should not be treated as a final sloping-site quote. Three-storey and unusual access remain site-specific.

sections.title: How long will the access be needed?

blocks.text: Coordinate the hire period with all trades. Roofing may finish before painting, cladding or window work. Confirm the starting event for rental, any minimum hire and the dismantling notice period.

sections.title: What should you request from a scaffolder?

items: A marked-up coverage plan and working heights.
Platform width and intended users/trades.
Edge protection, gates, stairs and loading requirements included.
Flat, sloping or restricted-access assumptions.
Delivery, erection, inspection, alteration and dismantling scope.
Included hire, extra weekly rate, GST and any permissions or engineering exclusions.

faqs.q: Is the estimator’s four-week hire period an industry rule?
faqs.a: No. It is the tool’s planning assumption. A scaffolder’s actual quote may use a different included or minimum period.

compare-quotes.title: How to compare roofing quotes in New Zealand
compare-quotes.description: Compare NZ roofing quotes on the same GST basis and scope, check products, access, removal, flashings and exclusions, and understand when two prices are not directly comparable.
compare-quotes.answer: Start by making the quotes comparable, not by choosing the lowest total. Put every quote on the same GST basis, confirm the same roofing product and major scope items, then compare exclusions, warranties, programme and contractor information. Consumer Protection and RANZ both warn that differences in price can reflect different scope, materials or approaches rather than a simple quality ranking.

sections.title: How do you make two roofing quotes comparable?

items: Confirm whether each total includes GST.
Confirm the proposed roofing system, profile, coating or finish and any stated thickness or grade.
Match removal and disposal of the existing roof.
Match scaffold, edge protection and difficult-access allowances.
Match underlay, flashings, penetrations and rainwater work.
Identify timber, substrate or structural repairs that are excluded or provisional.
Record warranties, programme, payment terms and the process for variations.

blocks.text: New Zealand GST is 15%. RoofHub only normalises a quote when you tell us whether its amount includes or excludes GST. An unknown GST basis is a reason to stop the price comparison, not a reason to guess.

blocks.title: Check a quote you already have
blocks.text: Enter the amount, GST basis and major scope items. RoofHub will show whether the quote is comparable with the project information you have supplied before showing a price-position label.
blocks.label: Open Quote Checker

sections.title: What is the difference between a quote and an estimate?

blocks.caption: Quote versus estimate

cells: Quote
An offer to do specified work for a stated price once accepted.
Exact scope, exclusions and how variations will be agreed.
Estimate
A best estimate or range based on the information and assumptions available.
Limits, assumptions and what could cause the final price to change.

blocks.text: Commerce Commission guidance says extra work outside an accepted quote needs customer agreement before the price changes. For estimates, significant possible variation and its conditions should be made clear.

sections.title: Why can roofing quotes be far apart?

blocks.text: RANZ notes that differences may come from what is included, which roofing material or system is proposed, and how the work will be carried out. Consumer Protection similarly recommends looking beyond price at experience, reliability, quality standards, references and past projects.

A quote sitting above or below a RoofHub indicative range is not proof that the contractor is expensive, cheap, good or bad. Different scope, access, specification, timing and site conditions can change the total.
If the totals are far apart, ask each contractor to explain the scope in writing. A clearer quote is often more useful than a lower headline number with unresolved exclusions.

sections.title: When does the written building contract threshold matter?

blocks.text: For residential building work costing $30,000 or more including GST, Building Performance says a written contract is required. The contractor must also provide the consumer protection standard checklist and disclosure statement at that threshold, or if the homeowner asks for them.

A roofing quote and a building contract are related but not interchangeable documents. The accepted scope should flow into the contract, including payment, variations, responsibilities and any exclusions that matter to the project.

sections.title: What should you do before accepting a roofing quote?

items: Resolve any unknown GST basis.
Ask for the exact roof product or system where the description is vague.
Make major inclusions and exclusions explicit.
Ask what could become a variation and who approves it.
Check relevant experience, references and business information.
Read warranty conditions rather than comparing warranty years alone.
For residential building work at or above the statutory threshold, make sure the written contract and required disclosure information are in place.

blocks.title: Still comparing the numbers?
blocks.text: Use the Quote Checker for scope alignment, or estimate the same roof independently before deciding what questions to take back to the contractor.
blocks.label: Check my roofing quote

faqs.q: Does the lowest roofing quote mean the best value?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Compare the same roof system and scope, then consider contractor experience, reliability, quality standards, references, warranties and the proposed way of carrying out the work.

faqs.q: Should a roofing quote include GST?
faqs.a: Commerce Commission guidance says quotes or estimates should be inclusive of GST. If a document is unclear, ask the contractor before comparing totals.

new-roof-cost.title: New roof cost NZ: what should a new-build roof budget include?
new-roof-cost.description: Plan a new-build roof budget in NZ without mixing in reroof removal costs. Compare roof area, profile, geometry, access, flashings, underlay, rainwater scope and current source-specific price guides.
new-roof-cost.answer: A new-build roof should be budgeted separately from a reroof because there is no old roof to strip and dispose of. Current public guides can provide context, but they are not a national tariff. Tasman Roofing's July 2026 contractor guide publishes $90-$180/m² for long-run steel as a fully installed range and a $15,000-$55,000 headline new-roof range. RoofHub keeps those figures attached to that source and its Auckland-oriented context rather than turning them into an automatic estimator rate.

sections.title: How is new-roof pricing different from reroof pricing?

blocks.caption: New build and reroof are different scopes

cells: Existing roof removal
Normally not part of the roofing scope.
Often required and should be explicit.
Disposal
Usually limited to installation waste.
Old roofing and associated waste may be a major item.
Hidden existing-roof condition
Not an old-roof strip-out risk.
Battens, substrate or structure may only become fully visible after removal.
Programme
Coordinated with the new-build programme and other trades.
Often coordinated around keeping an existing building weathertight.

blocks.title: Start with a new-build estimate
blocks.text: Describe the roof you know now. RoofHub keeps the project as a new roof so removal uncertainty is not silently added.
blocks.label: Estimate a new roof

sections.title: What are NZ businesses publishing in 2026?

blocks.text: Tasman Roofing's July 2026 guide publishes a $15,000-$55,000 headline range for a new roof and $90-$180/m² for long-run steel described as fully installed. It also says roof size, material, pitch and access are major drivers. This is one contractor-authored guide, not a representative national survey.

The guide does not make the GST treatment of every displayed range explicit. RoofHub therefore leaves its figures on their published basis instead of silently adding or removing GST. Use the source as market context, then price a real roof on a stated scope.
RoofHub does not convert a contractor cost guide into the estimator rate card. Estimator rates stay behind a separate review and approval process.

sections.title: Which measurements change a new-roof budget?

items: Actual sloping roof area or a clearly identified footprint/floor-area starting point.
Pitch for each roof plane where it differs.
Ridge, hip, valley and barge lengths for a detailed estimate.
Profile and effective cover for sheet quantities.
Flashings, penetrations, internal gutters and other custom details.
Storeys, edge protection, crane or delivery constraints and site access.

blocks.text: Floor area is not automatically roof area. A two-storey building is the clearest trap: total building floor area can be much larger than the roof footprint. RoofHub asks what an area measurement represents before using it.

sections.title: What should be defined before comparing new-roof prices?

blocks.text: A useful comparison names the roofing system, profile, coating or finish, thickness or grade where relevant, underlay, flashings, penetrations, rainwater interfaces and who supplies each component. A generic “metal roof” allowance can hide specification differences before installation starts.

Tasman's guide also separates new installation from reroofing and identifies roof shape, pitch, access and material selection as cost drivers. RoofHub treats those as project facts, not universal percentage multipliers.

sections.title: How should a builder or designer use an early roof allowance?

blocks.text: Use an allowance to make the uncertainty visible. Record the assumed roof area, system, pitch, access and major included components, then replace approximations with measured quantities as the design develops. That makes the allowance auditable instead of making an early number look more precise than the information supports.

blocks.title: Already have roof measurements?
blocks.text: Move straight to the detailed estimator and replace approximate geometry with measured areas and component lengths.
blocks.label: Use measured quantities

faqs.q: Does a new-build roof budget include removing an old roof?
faqs.a: Normally no. Removal and disposal belong to reroof/replacement scope unless there is an unusual existing structure or demolition item that has been explicitly included.

faqs.q: Is $90-$180/m² a RoofHub estimator rate?
faqs.a: No. It is a source-specific range published in a July 2026 Tasman Roofing guide. RoofHub does not automatically promote published market guides into its estimator rate card.

membrane.title: Membrane roofing NZ: systems, falls, substrates and quote checks
membrane.description: Understand NZ membrane roofing systems including TPO, EPDM/butyl, torch-on bitumen and liquid membranes, with design, substrate, drainage, appraisal and quote-check questions.
membrane.answer: “Membrane roof” is not one product. New Zealand systems include TPO and other single-ply sheets, butyl or EPDM, torch-on modified bitumen and liquid-applied systems. The selected proprietary system determines compatible substrates, falls, details and installer requirements. BRANZ notes that membrane roofs can work at lower falls than many other roofing materials, but a generic minimum should not replace the requirements of the selected system or consent pathway.

sections.title: Which membrane roof systems are used in New Zealand?

blocks.caption: Common membrane families

cells: TPO / other thermoplastic single-ply
Sheet membrane with welded seams.
Named system, membrane thickness, attachment, compatible substrate, details and approved accessories.
Butyl / EPDM
Flexible synthetic-rubber sheet systems.
System appraisal or technical literature, substrate, adhesive/joints, falls and installer requirements.
Torch-on modified bitumen
Bituminous membrane, commonly multi-layered.
Layer build-up, substrate, fire-safe installation process, outlets and detailing.
Liquid-applied
Applied coating built to a specified membrane thickness.
Substrate preparation, application thickness, curing/site conditions and compatible details.

blocks.text: A membrane family is not a specification. The quote should name the proprietary system and build-up, not only say “membrane roofing”.

sections.title: How much fall does a membrane roof need?

blocks.text: BRANZ explains that roofs designed to E2/AS1 have a minimum fall of 2 degrees and recommends 3 degrees in its general membrane article to preserve drainage as buildings and substrates move over time. That is general guidance, not permission to substitute one system for another.

Product-specific evidence can use different ways of expressing fall. For example, the Rubco Butyl BRANZ appraisal lists a minimum roof fall of 1:30 within its stated scope and also specifies substrate and wind limitations. Always check the current document for the exact system being proposed.
Falls, outlets, overflows, internal gutters and junctions work as one drainage design. A low-slope roof cannot be assessed from membrane brand alone.

sections.title: Why does the substrate matter so much?

blocks.text: Membranes rely on a continuous substrate and detailed junctions. The accepted substrate varies by system and may include treated plywood, proprietary roof sarking or concrete within stated conditions. Movement joints, penetrations and transitions need system-compatible detailing.

items: Identify the exact substrate and treatment/specification.
Confirm the membrane system is approved or supported for that substrate.
Check falls before the membrane is installed, not only after.
Coordinate outlets, overflows, parapets, penetrations and internal gutters.
Confirm protection where later trades or maintenance traffic could damage the membrane.
Use the system supplier's current details and required installer pathway.

sections.title: How should membrane roofing be priced?

blocks.text: Membrane pricing is unusually sensitive to substrate preparation, perimeter and upstand detailing, outlets, penetrations, insulation or warm-roof build-up, protection and the selected proprietary system. An area-only rate can hide too much of the job.

RoofHub does not currently publish a membrane result from its estimator. The shared project taxonomy supports membrane roofing, but there is no approved membrane estimator rate path yet. That is deliberate: the tool will not invent a price to fill the gap.

blocks.title: Describe the roof without inventing a price
blocks.text: You can still save membrane as the desired roof system and capture shape, size and project context. RoofHub will show that pricing is not configured rather than substituting a metal-roof rate.
blocks.label: Start a membrane roof project

sections.title: What should you look for in a membrane roofing quote?

items: Exact proprietary membrane system and membrane thickness/build-up.
Substrate and any preparation, replacement or levelling allowance.
Designed falls and drainage outlets/overflows.
Perimeters, upstands, parapets, penetrations and internal gutter details.
Insulation or warm-roof components if applicable.
Required approved or trained installer status.
Warranty documents, maintenance conditions and excluded traffic/protection work.
Scaffold/access and any separately priced building work.

blocks.title: Compare the scope before the headline price
blocks.text: If you already have a membrane quote, use Quote Checker to record GST and major project scope. Treat the result as a scope/comparability check, not a substitute for membrane-specific technical review.
blocks.label: Check my quote

faqs.q: Is TPO the same as every membrane roof?
faqs.a: No. TPO is one membrane family. Butyl/EPDM, modified-bitumen torch-on, PVC/KEE and liquid-applied systems have different products and build-ups.

faqs.q: Why does RoofHub not show a membrane estimate yet?
faqs.a: The current RoofHub estimator has no approved membrane rate pathway. Rather than map membrane work onto a metal-roof model or an unsupported market average, RoofHub leaves the price unconfigured until the calculation method and evidence are reviewed.

reroof-consent.title: Do you need building consent to reroof in NZ?
reroof-consent.description: Understand when replacing roof cladding in New Zealand may be exempt from building consent, when the exemption can fail, and when LBP or council advice is needed.
reroof-consent.answer: A straightforward reroof can be exempt from building consent when it is genuine repair or replacement using a comparable component in the same position and the work meets the Schedule 1 conditions. That is not a blanket exemption. If the roof or relevant assembly failed its Building Code durability requirement, the proposed work is not comparable, or the project goes beyond the exemption, consent or specific advice may be required. All work must still comply with the Building Code.

sections.title: What is the basic consent test for a reroof?

blocks.caption: Common reroof situations

cells: Older roof cladding has reached normal service life and is replaced with comparable cladding in the same position
This can fall within the general repair, maintenance and replacement exemption if all conditions are met.
Confirm the full scope remains within the exemption and Building Code requirements.
Roof or relevant assembly failed before meeting its required durability
The Schedule 1 repair/replacement exemption does not cover repair or replacement of a component that failed Building Code durability requirements.
Check the consent position before work starts.
Material, structure, roof form or other scope changes materially
The comparable-replacement test may no longer fit the work.
Ask the council or an appropriately qualified professional to confirm the pathway.
You are unsure
Owners are responsible for deciding whether work is exempt.
Use the government consent checker and confirm uncertainty with the council or a suitable professional.

blocks.text: Exempt from building consent does not mean exempt from the Building Code. The work still has to comply with the Building Code and other applicable requirements.

sections.title: Why does the age and failure history of the roof matter?

blocks.text: Building Performance gives an example of 20-year-old profiled metal cladding that has achieved its durability requirement and can be replaced with comparable profiled metal roofing under the exemption. The same guidance excludes repair or replacement where a component failed to satisfy the Building Code durability provisions.
That distinction is why a leaking roof should not automatically be treated as a routine consent-exempt replacement. The cause, age, assembly and proposed remedy can matter.

sections.title: When does a Licensed Building Practitioner matter?

blocks.text: Restricted building work is residential work that is consented and affects primary structure or weathertightness. Where roofing work is restricted building work, an appropriately licensed LBP must carry out or supervise that work and provide the required records.

Not every reroof is restricted building work, and not every exempt reroof requires an LBP for the same legal reason. Use the actual consent and RBW status of the project rather than treating "LBP" as a universal yes/no badge.

sections.title: What should you confirm before work starts?

items: Whether the existing roof is old enough and sound enough for the general replacement exemption to be relevant.
Whether the proposed cladding and assembly are genuinely comparable or involve a material design change.
Whether structural, fire-safety, drainage, penetrations or other building work is being added to the reroof.
Whether the work is restricted building work and who holds the appropriate licence if it is.
Whether your council has any project-specific requirements or advice.

blocks.title: Planning a replacement roof?
blocks.text: Estimate the replacement scope first, then keep consent and site-specific requirements visible as separate project checks.
blocks.label: Estimate a reroof

sections.title: What RoofHub cannot decide from an online question

blocks.text: RoofHub can explain the national guidance, but it cannot inspect the building, determine why a roof failed, decide whether two assemblies are legally comparable, or issue a consent exemption. For uncertain, unusual or failed-roof cases, confirm the position before physical work starts.

faqs.q: Does replacing an old metal roof always need a building consent in NZ?
faqs.a: No. Comparable repair or replacement in the same position can be exempt if the Schedule 1 conditions are met. Important exceptions apply, including work on components that failed Building Code durability requirements.

faqs.q: Does consent-exempt roofing work still have to meet the Building Code?
faqs.a: Yes. Building Performance states that all building work must comply with the Building Code even where a building consent exemption applies.

faqs.q: Can RoofHub tell me whether my specific reroof is exempt?
faqs.a: RoofHub can explain the published rules but cannot determine the legal status of an unseen building. Use the government checker and confirm uncertain cases with your council or an appropriately qualified professional.

repair-or-replace.title: Roof repair or replacement: how to decide in NZ
repair-or-replace.description: A neutral NZ repair-vs-restoration-vs-reroof decision framework using roof condition, failure spread and repeat history rather than a sales-first or age-only answer.
repair-or-replace.answer: Start with the smallest intervention that can fix the underlying problem durably. A local defect on an otherwise serviceable roof can justify targeted repair; a sound roof with mainly surface deterioration can sometimes be restored; widespread corrosion, multiple failing areas or repeated failures across the roof make replacement more plausible. Age alone is not the decision, and hidden condition still needs competent assessment.

sections.title: Repair, restore or replace: what is the actual decision?

blocks.caption: Three different interventions solve three different kinds of problem

cells: Targeted repair
A defect is localised and the surrounding roof remains serviceable.
The actual water-entry/failure point, compatibility of the repair and nearby roof condition.
Restoration / recoating
The roof system is fundamentally suitable and the main issue is surface/coating deterioration after necessary repairs.
Substrate condition, fixings, flashings, underlay/detailing where relevant, and coating-system suitability.
Replacement / reroof
Deterioration is widespread, failures recur across different areas, material is beyond useful repair, or the work needed to make the old system reliable becomes disproportionate.
Hidden substrate/framing, asbestos/safety constraints, replacement specification and opening-up allowances.

blocks.title: How working NZ roofers describe the same decision
blocks.synthesis: The practitioner evidence points to a proportional rule rather than a sales-first rule: local problems can justify local work; a serviceable roof with surface wear may justify restoration; broad failure makes replacement more plausible. RoofHub deliberately records whether a source sells repair, restoration or replacement so repeated commercial recommendations are not mistaken for independent proof.

sections.title: The five questions RoofHub uses before pointing toward a pathway

items: What roof system is it: long-run metal, concrete tile, pressed metal tile, membrane or something else?
Is the problem in one local area, several separate areas, or widespread across the roof?
Is this the first occurrence, the same repair failing again, or different areas failing over time?
From a safe location, is the visible issue mainly surface wear, local damage, holes/missing material, or sagging/movement?
Are there asbestos or brittle-roofing concerns that change how the roof can be investigated or disturbed?

blocks.text: RoofHub does not use a universal roof-age or percentage-damaged rule. The same age can describe very different remaining condition depending on roof system, exposure, detailing, maintenance and installation history.

sections.title: “Cheapest” should mean the lowest adequate intervention, not the lowest invoice today

blocks.text: A patch is good value when it actually addresses a contained failure and the surrounding roof remains serviceable. It is false economy when the same type of failure is appearing across the roof or when the repair leaves known system-wide defects untouched. The reverse is also true: replacing a whole roof solely because one repairable flashing or sheet failed can be unnecessary scope.

When contractor recommendations differ, ask each contractor to identify the defect they are solving, what surrounding condition they observed, what they are excluding, and what they expect the proposed intervention not to fix. That makes repair, restoration and reroof proposals easier to compare on scope rather than sales language.

sections.title: What should a useful condition assessment cover?

items: Where water is likely entering, not only where the internal stain appears.
Roof cladding/tile/membrane condition and whether defects are isolated or repeated.
Fixings, cut edges, laps and corrosion where relevant.
Ridges, hips, valleys, barges, aprons, penetrations and other flashings.
Gutters, outlets and drainage paths.
Underlay, battens/purlins, substrate or framing where these can be inspected safely or become exposed during work.
Moisture/ventilation conditions where condensation may be involved.
Asbestos/brittle-roofing risk before cleaning, drilling, cutting or removal.

blocks.text: Ask RoofHub about what you can see safely. The Assistant can use a condition-triage framework to separate plausible repair, restoration, replacement and “needs inspection” pathways without pretending it has inspected the roof.

sections.title: Compare the proposed scope before comparing the price

blocks.text: A repair quote and a reroof quote are not competing prices for the same scope. If the condition is borderline, ask for the repair/restoration limitations in writing and compare what each option includes, excludes and leaves for later.

blocks.text: Keep the covering estimate separate from unresolved opening-up work. Hidden timber, substrate damage, asbestos and design changes should remain explicit allowances or uncertainties rather than being silently assumed to cost zero.

faqs.q: Should I replace my roof after one leak?
faqs.a: Not automatically. One leak can come from a local flashing, penetration, valley, sheet/tile defect or moisture issue. The surrounding roof condition and whether the failure is isolated matter more than the existence of one leak.

faqs.q: Will RoofHub always recommend the cheapest option?
faqs.a: RoofHub aims for the lowest adequate intervention: the least scope that can reasonably address the underlying problem without leaving known system-wide failure behind. That may be a repair, restoration or replacement depending on condition.

faqs.q: Does an old roof automatically need replacement?
faqs.a: No. Age is context, not a diagnosis. Condition, failure pattern, repairability, material/system limits and hidden substrate or safety issues are more useful decision inputs.

leak-condensation.title: Roof leak or condensation? How to tell what to investigate
leak-condensation.description: Learn why ceiling stains and roof-space moisture do not always mean the roof is leaking, what observations help distinguish rain entry from condensation, and when to call a professional.
leak-condensation.answer: Water inside a building can come from external rain entry, condensation, plumbing or another source, and the stain may be some distance from the cause. Rain-linked, localised wetting around a penetration or flashing points the investigation in a different direction from widespread moisture on the underside of cold roofing or underlay. Do not choose a reroof, sealant repair or ventilation product until the source has been investigated.
intents: is my roof leaking or is it condensation
why is underside of roof wet

sections.title: What clues help separate a roof leak from condensation?

blocks.caption: Useful observations before diagnosis

cells: Moisture appears during or soon after wind-driven rain and is localised near a roof junction, penetration or flashing
External water entry
Water can travel along framing or underlay before it becomes visible, so the stain is not proof of the entry point.
Widespread droplets or dampness beneath cold roof cladding or underlay, especially with high internal humidity
Condensation/internal moisture
Condensation and leaks can occur together; a roof-space inspection may be needed.
Moisture persists independently of weather
Plumbing, internal moisture or another source
RoofHub cannot identify the source remotely.
Blocked or overflowing gutters during rain
Drainage problem that can contribute to water entry
The overflow cause and drainage capacity still need checking.

sections.title: What causes roof-space condensation?

blocks.text: MRM explains that moisture produced inside a building can enter the ceiling cavity. When metal or another surface is cold enough, water vapour can condense. Persistent moisture can affect underlay, timber, fasteners, insulation and roof cladding.

BRANZ describes roof-space ventilation as primarily a moisture-management measure in New Zealand. Ventilation design depends on roof and ceiling type, moisture sources and the construction, so adding a vent without understanding the moisture pathway is not a complete diagnosis.

sections.title: Where do external roof leaks commonly need investigation?

blocks.text: Flashings are designed to divert water away from potential entry points. Ridges, hips, valleys, barges/verges, aprons, parapets and penetrations all create details that may need inspection when rain entry is suspected.

Complex junctions can involve several overlapping flashings and interfaces. BRANZ roof-junction details illustrate why simply sealing the visible line is not always equivalent to repairing the water-management detail.

sections.title: What can you check safely before calling someone?

items: Note whether the moisture follows rain, cold weather, showers/cooking or another pattern.
Photograph stains and visible roof-space moisture without disturbing materials.
Check gutters and downpipes from ground level for obvious blockage or overflow signs.
Record nearby skylights, chimneys, vents, valleys or wall junctions.
If older textured tiles may contain asbestos, do not clean, drill, cut or waterblast them as a test.

blocks.text: Do not climb onto a roof to chase a leak. Working at height needs appropriate competence and controls, and suspect asbestos introduces a separate hazard.

sections.title: What should the next professional visit answer?

items: What is the most likely moisture source?
What evidence supports that conclusion?
Is the defect local or system-wide?
Does the roof space have an internal-moisture problem as well as any external leak?
What repair scope is proposed, and what would remain unresolved?

blocks.title: If replacement is being discussed
blocks.text: Build an independent RoofHub reroof range from the roof you know, then compare the contractor scope separately.
blocks.label: Estimate a reroof

faqs.q: Can condensation look like a roof leak?
faqs.a: Yes. Roof-space condensation can create droplets, damp insulation or staining, while external water can also travel before it appears. The moisture source needs investigation rather than diagnosis from the stain alone.

faqs.q: Will adding roof vents fix condensation?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Ventilation can be part of moisture management, but the correct response depends on moisture sources, air movement, insulation and the roof/ceiling construction.

roof-underlay.title: Roof underlay in NZ: what it does on a metal roof
roof-underlay.description: Understand roofing underlay under NZ metal roofs, its role in condensation management, why it is not a second roof, and what changes during reroofing.
roof-underlay.answer: Underlay beneath profiled metal roofing is primarily part of moisture management. Current NZ Metal Roofing Manufacturers guidance says absorbent roofing underlay temporarily contains condensation and releases it when conditions allow; it is not a reliable drainage plane or a substitute for weatherproof roof detailing. On reroofs, existing underlay should not simply be buried under a new layer unless the retained support is in as-new condition, and MRM recommends no more than one compliant underlay layer apart from laps.
intents: what does roof underlay do
do i need new underlay when reroofing

sections.title: What is roofing underlay supposed to do?

blocks.text: MRM describes the role of absorbent roof underlay as temporarily absorbing condensation and later releasing that moisture back to the atmosphere. It also contributes to pressure equalisation and moisture management within the assembly.

Underlay is not a second waterproof roof. Fastener penetrations, purlins and the way condensation forms mean it should not be relied on to carry water to the gutter instead of proper roof and flashing design.

sections.title: What happens to underlay during a reroof?

blocks.text: Current MRM guidance says that with reroofs, it is not acceptable to lay the new roof over existing underlay or underlay support unless the retained material is in as-new condition. Its reroof bulletin also recommends no more than a single compliant layer of underlay, apart from laps, under profiled metal roofing.
That means a quote that simply says "new roof over existing paper" deserves clarification. The condition, type and intended build-up should be explicit.

sections.title: Can underlay solve a condensation problem by itself?

blocks.text: No. If the moisture load exceeds what the assembly can manage, underlay can become saturated and other roof-space materials can remain wet. MRM says the response is to reduce moisture entering the cavity and/or improve the relevant ventilation pathway, depending on the design.
BRANZ similarly frames roof-space ventilation as moisture management above the ceiling insulation and below the roof cladding, not as a generic add-on for every roof.

sections.title: What should an underlay line in a roofing quote tell you?

items: Named underlay product or at least the required performance/type.
Whether the existing underlay/support is removed or retained, and why.
How the underlay interfaces with eaves, ridges, penetrations and any ventilation strategy.
Whether added insulation or a changed roof build-up affects moisture design.
Any fire, support or project-specific requirements that apply.

blocks.title: Compare the rest of the reroof scope
blocks.text: Use Quote Checker to line up underlay, removal, flashings, access and other major inclusions before comparing price.
blocks.label: Check a roofing quote

sections.title: Why product and project requirements still matter

blocks.text: Underlay requirements vary with cladding systems and the project compliance path. RoofHub explains the general role; the designer, roofer, supplier or consent documents need to confirm the actual product and installation requirements for the building.

faqs.q: Does roof underlay drain condensation into the gutter?
faqs.a: That is not its primary role. MRM specifically warns against treating underlay as a drainage plane or a second roof; it is intended to absorb moisture temporarily and release it when conditions allow.

faqs.q: Can a roofer put new underlay over the old underlay?
faqs.a: Current MRM guidance says a reroof should not be laid over existing underlay or support unless the retained material is in as-new condition, and recommends no more than one compliant underlay layer apart from laps.

roof-flashings.title: Roof flashings explained: ridge, hip, valley, barge and apron
roof-flashings.description: A plain-English NZ guide to the main roof flashing names, where they occur, what they do and why flashing length and complexity matter in measurements and quotes.
roof-flashings.answer: Flashings manage water at roof edges, changes of direction and junctions. On metal roofs, common line flashings include ridge and hip flashings, barge or verge flashings, apron flashings and valleys; parapet cappings and penetration details add other types. These are not decorative lines. Each one exists because a roof changes plane, meets a wall or needs a weatherproof termination, which is why complex roofs need more lineal detailing than simple roofs of the same area.
intents: what is a roof valley
what is a barge flashing
what flashings does my roof need

sections.title: What are the main roof flashing types?

blocks.caption: Common roof lines and what they mean

cells: Ridge
High line where two roof planes meet.
Closes and weatherproofs the meeting of the roof planes.
Hip
Sloping external line where two roof planes meet.
Weatherproofs the external intersection and covers cut sheet edges.
Valley
Internal line where two roof planes drain toward each other.
Receives and carries concentrated roof water while protecting the internal junction.
Barge / verge
Sloping outside edge of a gable roof.
Closes and weatherproofs the side edge of the roofing.
Apron
Where a roof surface meets an adjacent wall or similar upstand.
Turns water away from the wall/roof junction.
Parapet capping
Top of a parapet wall.
Protects the top of the wall from moisture entry.

sections.title: Why do flashings change roofing cost and labour?

blocks.text: A simple gable can have a large roof area but relatively few junctions. A smaller cut-up roof can have several valleys, hips, wall junctions and penetrations. Those details require additional measured lengths, cutting, folding, joining and weatherproofing work, so roof area alone does not describe the full scope.
BRANZ roof-junction examples show how several flashing pieces can interact at one junction. This is why RoofHub keeps lineal roof components separate from square metres in the detailed estimator.

sections.title: How do roof shapes create ridges, hips and valleys?

items: A simple gable normally has a ridge and two barge/verge edges.
A hip roof adds sloping hip lines and may have a shorter ridge.
Intersecting gables create valleys where inward-facing planes meet.
Hip-and-valley roofs combine external hips and internal valleys.
Dormers and multiple roof sections can add ridges, valleys, aprons, barges and penetration-style junctions.

blocks.text: The diagram or roof-shape name is a geometry aid, not an installation specification. Actual flashing widths, laps, materials and detailing depend on the roof profile, pitch, exposure and junction.

sections.title: What should you look for in a quote?

items: Are major flashings included or excluded?
Are valleys and wall/apron junctions identified where the roof has them?
Are skylights, chimneys, vents and other penetrations included?
Are replacement gutters/spouting being confused with roof flashings?
If existing flashings are to be reused, is that assumption explicit?

blocks.title: Have real roof measurements?
blocks.text: The detailed estimator keeps roof area, ridges, hips, valleys, barges and other components as separate quantities.
blocks.label: Use measurements

sections.title: Can a leaking flashing just be sealed?

blocks.text: Sometimes a local repair is appropriate, but sealant is not a substitute for a correctly designed and installed water-management detail. The defect, material compatibility, lap arrangement and surrounding construction need to be understood first.

faqs.q: Is a valley the same thing as a gutter?
faqs.a: No. A roof valley is an internal roof junction that carries concentrated water between roof planes. A gutter or spouting collects water at an eave or other drainage edge and discharges it to outlets/downpipes.

faqs.q: Is barge the same as verge?
faqs.a: The terms are commonly paired for the flashing at the sloping outside edge of a gable. MRM groups Barge and Verge together as a flashing type.

choose-roofer.title: How to choose a roofer in New Zealand
choose-roofer.description: A practical NZ checklist for checking roofing contractors, licensing where required, references, written scope, contracts, safety, warranties and quote comparability.
choose-roofer.answer: Choose a roofer by checking the company and the people who will actually do or supervise the work, then compare written scope rather than relying on one headline price. For residential work that is restricted building work, the relevant work must be done or supervised by an appropriately licensed LBP. For residential building work costing $30,000 or more including GST, a written contract is required, with statutory disclosure/checklist requirements at that threshold or when requested.

how to check a roofing company
does my roofer need to be licensed

sections.title: What should you check before choosing a roofer?

items: Legal business name and contact details.
Who will carry out or supervise the roofing work.
Relevant roofing experience and recent comparable projects.
References you can contact.
Appropriate LBP status where the work is restricted building work.
Public liability or other relevant insurance information and what it covers.
A written scope showing product, removal, access, flashings, underlay, drainage work and exclusions.
Warranty terms and maintenance conditions.
Payment schedule, start assumptions and variation process.

blocks.text: Building Performance recommends checking references, obtaining more than one quote, using a written agreement and checking the appropriate licence where restricted building work applies.

sections.title: Does every roofer need to be an LBP?

blocks.text: The legal requirement depends on the work. Restricted building work is residential work in the relevant consent/RBW framework that affects primary structure or weathertightness. Where the roofing work is RBW, an appropriately licensed LBP must do or supervise it.

For work outside that category, a roofing licence is not automatically the only measure of competence. Experience, scope, references, safety systems, product knowledge and contract quality still matter.

sections.title: How many quotes should you get and how should you compare them?

blocks.text: Building Performance recommends presenting the project to at least three contractors and reviewing the quotes before signing. Consumer Protection also recommends several written quotes where practical. The useful comparison is like-for-like scope, not just the cheapest total.

blocks.title: Already have a quote?
blocks.text: Normalize GST and line up the roof system, removal, scaffold, underlay, flashings and other major scope before judging the price.
blocks.label: Check a quote

sections.title: When is a written building contract mandatory?

blocks.text: Building Performance says residential building work costing $30,000 or more including GST must have a written contract. At that threshold, or if the homeowner asks, the contractor must provide the consumer-protection checklist and disclosure statement.
A detailed roofing quote can form part of the commercial scope, but it is not a substitute for every contract requirement on work where a written building contract is mandatory.

sections.title: What does trade-association membership tell you?

blocks.text: RANZ membership can be a useful industry signal and RANZ publishes consumer guidance and a roofer directory. Building Performance notes more generally that industry-association membership can indicate professionalism and experience, but does not replace a legal licence or qualification where one is required.

sections.title: What should make you ask more questions?

items: A quote with no clear roof product or major inclusions.
Pressure to accept immediately without time to read scope/terms.
Unclear GST treatment or payment schedule.
No explanation of who will actually perform or supervise the work.
No process for hidden timber damage or other variations.
Warranty years quoted without the actual warranty terms or maintenance obligations.
Requests to bypass consent or licensing requirements that appear to apply.

blocks.title: Prepare the project first
blocks.text: A clear brief makes quotes easier to compare and gives contractors fewer assumptions to fill in differently.
blocks.label: Prepare for a roofing quote

faqs.q: Should I only use a RANZ member roofer?
faqs.a: RANZ membership can be a useful industry signal, but RoofHub does not treat membership as the only test. Check the actual company, scope, references, people doing the work and any statutory licensing requirements that apply.

faqs.q: How do I check whether a roofer is a Licensed Building Practitioner?
faqs.a: Building Performance directs homeowners to the public LBP register. Check that the person is current and that the licence class is appropriate for the restricted building work involved.

faqs.q: Do I need a written contract for roofing work under $30,000?
faqs.a: The statutory threshold described by Building Performance is $30,000 or more including GST, but it recommends a written agreement even for lower-value work so obligations and expectations are clear.

roof-warranties.title: Roof warranties in NZ: product, workmanship and legal rights
roof-warranties.description: Understand the different protections behind a NZ roofing job: manufacturer product warranties, contractor workmanship warranties, Building Act implied warranties and maintenance conditions.
roof-warranties.answer: A roofing "warranty" can mean several different things. A manufacturer product warranty covers specified product performance under its terms; a roofer may provide separate workmanship or installation cover; and residential building work also has statutory implied warranties under the Building Act. These protections have different parties, conditions, claim processes and time periods, so compare the actual documents rather than the biggest number of years.

how long is a roof warranty
what are my rights if roofing work is defective

sections.title: What kinds of roofing warranty or protection can apply?

blocks.caption: Different protections answer different questions

cells: Manufacturer/product warranty
Product manufacturer or warranty provider.
Exact product, environment, application, coverage, exclusions, registration and maintenance conditions.
Workmanship / installation warranty
Roofing contractor or scheme named in the document.
What installation defects are covered, duration, transferability, exclusions and claim process.
Building Act implied warranties
Apply automatically to residential building work under the statutory framework.
The rights and remedies are legal protections, not a manufacturer marketing warranty.

sections.title: What are the Building Act implied warranties?

blocks.text: Building Performance says implied warranties apply to residential building work for up to 10 years regardless of whether there is a written contract or the project cost. They cover matters including Building Code compliance, good workmanship and completion within agreed or reasonable timeframes.

There is also an initial 12-month defect repair period. Building Performance explains that if a homeowner notifies the contractor in writing during that period, the contractor must put defective work right within a reasonable timeframe unless the contractor can show the issue is not their responsibility.

sections.title: Why do product warranties vary by location and environment?

blocks.text: Manufacturer warranties can depend on the selected product and environmental exposure. COLORSTEEL, for example, publishes environmental categories from mild through extremely severe and says product suitability, warranty and maintenance can vary with coastal proximity and local conditions.
A headline warranty duration is not a universal lifespan prediction. Read the actual warranty document for the named product, site environment and application.

sections.title: Can maintenance affect warranty coverage?

blocks.text: Yes, manufacturer warranty and care guidance can require inspection or cleaning, especially in sheltered or coastal areas. Keep the maintenance instructions and completion documents supplied with the job.

blocks.title: Build a maintenance plan
blocks.text: Use RoofHub maintenance guidance to understand what should be inspected and which tasks should be left to a professional.
blocks.label: Read roof maintenance guide

sections.title: What warranty questions belong in a quote comparison?

items: What exact product warranty document applies?
Who registers the product warranty and when?
What workmanship warranty is provided by the contractor?
What maintenance is required to preserve coverage?
Are coastal or special-environment conditions relevant?
What completion documents, producer statements, records or care instructions will be supplied?

blocks.text: Do not collapse all of those answers into a single "years of warranty" score. They cover different risks and may be provided by different parties.

faqs.q: Is a 30-year product warranty the same as a 30-year workmanship warranty?
faqs.a: No. Product and workmanship warranties are separate protections provided by different parties and can have different coverage, exclusions and claim processes.

faqs.q: Do NZ residential building works have legal warranties even without a written warranty document?
faqs.a: Building Performance says Building Act implied warranties apply automatically to residential building work for up to 10 years, regardless of whether there is a written contract.

faqs.q: Does coastal location affect a metal-roof warranty?
faqs.a: It can. Manufacturer guidance such as COLORSTEEL uses environmental categories and says product selection, warranty terms and maintenance can vary with coastal exposure and local conditions.

metal-roof-maintenance.title: Metal roof maintenance NZ: what to inspect and when
metal-roof-maintenance.description: A practical NZ guide to metal-roof maintenance, including gutters, valleys, debris, unwashed areas, coastal exposure, corrosion signs, safe inspection and asbestos cautions.
metal-roof-maintenance.answer: Metal roofs need periodic inspection and maintenance, but the correct frequency depends on the product, environment and roof details. Keep gutters and valleys clear, remove debris that traps moisture, pay attention to sheltered or unwashed areas, and deal with coating damage or corrosion before it becomes widespread. Coastal and severe micro-environments can need more frequent care. Work at height should be left to people with appropriate competence and safety controls.

sections.title: What should a metal-roof maintenance check cover?

items: Gutters, outlets and valleys for leaves, silt and other debris.
Sheltered areas that do not receive normal rain washing.
Visible corrosion, coating breakdown or staining.
Loose, damaged or missing flashings and obvious fastener issues.
Debris around solar equipment, penetrations and roof-mounted structures.
Downpipes and overflow paths for signs of blockage.
Nearby branches or materials that are rubbing, dropping debris or creating persistent wet areas.

blocks.text: RANZ and COLORSTEEL both emphasise drainage, debris and regular inspection. MRM also identifies vulnerable micro-environments and unwashed areas as maintenance concerns.

sections.title: How often should a metal roof be maintained?

blocks.text: There is no single RoofHub interval that overrides the product warranty. Frequency depends on exposure, product, roof geometry and whether surfaces are naturally rain-washed. COLORSTEEL publishes different maintenance expectations for different environmental categories, with sheltered areas requiring deliberate washing.
Use the maintenance schedule for the actual roof product and warranty. A generic annual checklist is useful for observation, but it is not a substitute for manufacturer-specific requirements.

sections.title: Why do coastal and sheltered areas need extra attention?

blocks.text: Salt and other contaminants can accumulate where rainfall does not wash the roof effectively. COLORSTEEL ties environmental severity and maintenance to exposure, while MRM describes severe marine micro-environments around eaves and other vulnerable areas.

blocks.title: Near the coast?
blocks.text: Check how environmental category, material compatibility and maintenance affect product selection and warranty.
blocks.label: Read coastal roofing guide

sections.title: What maintenance should not be a DIY roof walk?

blocks.text: RANZ warns that working at height needs proper competence and controls. RoofHub recommends ground-level observation, safe access to internal areas where appropriate, and professional roof access for tasks that require being on the roof.

If older textured roofing may contain asbestos, do not waterblast or use compressed air. WorkSafe published a 2026 safety alert after contamination incidents and specifically prohibits high-pressure water or compressed air on asbestos-containing material.

sections.title: What records are worth keeping?

items: Roof product and colour/coating.
Installation date and contractor.
Warranty and registration documents.
Manufacturer maintenance instructions.
Dates and photos of professional inspections or repairs.
Any roof-mounted equipment added later.
Invoices and scope for repairs that alter flashings, fixings or penetrations.

blocks.text: Building Performance says contractors must provide certain completion information for residential building work, including ongoing maintenance requirements and warranties/guarantees. Keeping those documents makes future maintenance and claims easier to interpret.

faqs.q: Can I waterblast a metal roof?
faqs.a: Roof cleaning methods depend on the roof material and condition. If older textured tiles or another material may contain asbestos, WorkSafe says high-pressure water spraying must not be used. For coated steel, follow the product manufacturer care instructions rather than a generic pressure-washing rule.

faqs.q: Do I need to wash a COLORSTEEL roof?
faqs.a: COLORSTEEL says sheltered areas that do not receive natural rain washing may need regular manual cleaning, and requirements vary with environment and application. Check the warranty/maintenance guide for the actual product and site.

coastal-roofing.title: Coastal roofing NZ: exposure, materials and maintenance
coastal-roofing.description: Understand how sea-salt exposure affects NZ metal roofing, product selection, warranties, compatible materials and maintenance without relying on one universal distance-from-coast rule.
coastal-roofing.answer: Coastal roofing should be specified for the actual exposure, not from a single nationwide distance rule. Manufacturer environmental categories use distance from salt water as one guide, but local wind, topography, building position and unwashed areas can change severity. Product/coating choice, compatible gutters and fasteners, detailing and maintenance all need to suit that environment.

sections.title: How is coastal exposure assessed?

blocks.text: COLORSTEEL publishes environmental categories from mild through extremely severe and states that distance from the coast is an important guide, while design, position and other local factors can change the appropriate product and warranty.
RoofHub does not turn distance-to-coast into an automatic product recommendation. Manufacturer confirmation may be needed for severe or unusual exposure.

sections.title: Why does material compatibility matter near the coast?

blocks.text: MRM warns that roof-envelope materials can corrode when incompatible metals are in contact or when runoff from one material reaches another. Gutters, fasteners, flashings, penetrations and roof-mounted equipment therefore need to be considered as part of one material system.

Copper and coated-steel combinations are a classic example of why runoff and contact need checking. The MRM compatibility table should be used for the actual material pairing rather than relying on appearance or generic "marine grade" language.

sections.title: What changes about maintenance in severe exposure?

blocks.text: Salt and contaminants can build up in sheltered and unwashed areas. Manufacturer maintenance schedules can become more demanding with environmental severity, and MRM recommends additional attention to vulnerable marine micro-environments such as eaves and roof undersides.

blocks.title: Build the maintenance side of the decision
blocks.text: Check gutters, valleys, sheltered areas and warranty-specific care requirements without treating maintenance as a substitute for correct product selection.
blocks.label: Read maintenance guide

sections.title: What should a coastal roofing quote specify?

items: Named roof product/coating, not only colour.
Any stated environmental category or manufacturer suitability confirmation.
Compatible flashings, fasteners, gutters and accessories.
Treatment of cut edges and vulnerable details where relevant to the system.
Maintenance and warranty conditions for the site.
How solar, aerials, vents or other roof-mounted items will avoid incompatible contact/runoff.

blocks.text: Warranty length should not be compared without checking the product, environment and required maintenance.

sections.title: Is one roofing material always best at the coast?

blocks.text: No. RoofHub does not rank a universal coastal winner. Suitability depends on the named product system, environment, compatible accessories, detailing, building design and maintenance. Use manufacturer and project-specific technical guidance for the final specification.

faqs.q: How close to the sea is considered coastal for roofing?
faqs.a: There is no single RoofHub cutoff. Manufacturer guides use distance bands but also warn that prevailing wind, local conditions, design and position can extend or change the exposure category.

faqs.q: Can copper gutters be used with coated steel roofing?
faqs.a: Material compatibility must be checked carefully. MRM identifies contact and runoff combinations that can cause corrosion and gives specific cautions around copper and coated steel.

gutters-downpipes.title: Gutters and downpipes NZ: what determines roof drainage capacity
gutters-downpipes.description: Understand the NZ factors behind gutter and downpipe sizing, including roof catchment, pitch, rainfall intensity, outlets, overflows, maintenance and material compatibility.
gutters-downpipes.answer: Gutter and downpipe capacity is not determined by house size alone. A roof drainage design has to account for the catchment draining to each section, roof geometry, local design rainfall, outlet/downpipe arrangement and the applicable compliance path. Blockage, poor fall or undersized outlets can also make an otherwise adequate system overflow, so maintenance and overflow behaviour matter as well as nominal gutter dimensions.

why are my gutters overflowing

sections.title: What determines gutter and downpipe capacity?

items: The roof catchment draining to each gutter section.
Roof pitch and geometry where required by the sizing method.
Local design rainfall intensity.
Gutter cross-section, fall and effective length.
Number, size and location of outlets/downpipes.
Overflow route and whether an internal gutter can discharge safely if blocked.
Any additional upper-roof discharge onto lower catchments.

blocks.text: E1/AS1 provides one NZ compliance pathway for roof drainage and BRANZ explains how roof drainage design depends on rainfall intensity and the actual gutter/outlet arrangement.

sections.title: Why does local rainfall intensity matter?

blocks.text: The same roof area can require different drainage capacity in different design rainfall conditions. BRANZ notes that external gutters need to be designed for the relevant 10-minute rainfall intensity, not less than the baseline used by the compliance method, and higher values may apply by location.
RoofHub does not size a specific gutter or downpipe from a national rule of thumb. Use the current compliance method and location-specific rainfall information for design.

sections.title: Why are overflows and internal gutters higher risk?

blocks.text: BRANZ highlights the need for suitable capacity, downpipes and overflow provisions, especially where internal gutters or rainwater heads are used. An overflow should not simply move water into the building when a primary outlet blocks or is exceeded.

sections.title: What maintenance problems reduce drainage performance?

blocks.text: Leaves, sediment and other debris can obstruct gutters, valleys and outlets. RANZ identifies blocked overflows and drainage issues as maintenance concerns, while COLORSTEEL recommends removing debris from gutters and valleys to avoid trapped moisture.

blocks.title: Roof showing moisture or overflow?
blocks.text: Separate drainage symptoms from roof leaks or condensation before deciding what work is needed.
blocks.label: Read leak vs condensation guide

sections.title: Do gutter and roof materials need to be compatible?

blocks.text: Yes. MRM warns that dissimilar metals can cause corrosion through direct contact or runoff. The drainage system, roof cladding and adjoining flashings should be treated as interacting materials rather than independent purchases.

faqs.q: How many downpipes does my roof need?
faqs.a: There is no reliable national answer from floor area alone. Outlet/downpipe sizing and quantity depend on the roof catchment, local rainfall intensity, gutter arrangement and the applicable design method.

faqs.q: Can blocked gutters cause roof leaks?
faqs.a: Blocked or overflowing drainage can contribute to water entry and damage, but the actual path still needs diagnosis. Clearing the blockage does not prove that every ceiling stain came from the gutter.

quote-prep.title: How to prepare for a roofing quote in New Zealand
quote-prep.description: What to gather before a roofing site visit, how to describe the roof and problem, and which scope, safety, contract, warranty and variation questions make quotes easier to compare.
quote-prep.answer: You do not need perfect measurements before asking for a roofing quote. Give the contractor the property location, what you know about the existing roof, the problem or outcome you want, safe photos/plans if available, storeys and access constraints. Then ask for the product and major scope in writing, including removal, scaffold or edge protection, underlay, flashings, penetrations, drainage work, likely variations and GST. Clear inputs make competing quotes much easier to compare.

what should a roofing quote include

sections.title: What should you tell the roofer before the site visit?

items: Property suburb/town and building type.

Scaffold, edge protection and other access costs.
Roofing product/profile/coating and any relevant thickness or grade.
Underlay and any substrate/batten work.
Ridges, hips, valleys, barges, aprons and penetration flashings.
Gutters, spouting, downpipes or drainage work if included.
Known timber/structural repairs and how hidden damage becomes a variation.
Freight, permits/consent work where relevant and GST.

blocks.text: Ask who will carry out or supervise the roofing, what comparable work they have done, and for references. Where the work is restricted building work, check the relevant LBP status. Building Performance also recommends discussing insurance, project role and subcontractors.

sections.title: How should hidden or uncertain work be handled?

blocks.text: Some roof conditions cannot be fully confirmed before strip-off, such as concealed timber or substrate damage. Ask how those discoveries become variations, what evidence will be provided and who must approve additional work before it proceeds. Consumer guidance on quotes also distinguishes the agreed quote scope from later extra work.

If older Decramastic/textured tiles may contain asbestos, identify that uncertainty before cleaning or removal. WorkSafe says high-pressure water and compressed air must not be used on asbestos-containing material.

sections.title: When do contract and consumer-protection requirements apply?

blocks.text: For residential building work costing $30,000 or more including GST, Building Performance says a written contract is mandatory. The contractor must provide the standard consumer checklist and disclosure statement at that threshold, or when the homeowner asks for them.

sections.title: What should you have before accepting?

items: A written roof product/system and clear major scope.
GST basis and payment schedule.
Known exclusions and provisional/variation process.
Expected timing or programme assumptions.
Warranty documents or at least the named warranties that will apply.
Consent/LBP position where relevant.
Who is responsible for site safety, scaffold and specialist work.
Enough information to compare the quote like-for-like with alternatives.

blocks.text: RANZ and Consumer Protection both emphasise that differences between quotes can reflect different scope and work methods. Clarity before acceptance is more useful than choosing a total you cannot explain.

faqs.q: Do I need roof measurements before getting a quote?
faqs.a: No. Measurements or plans help, but a contractor can inspect the site. What matters is that any missing information and assumptions remain clear so quotes can later be compared on the same basis.

faqs.q: Should I tell the roofer I am getting other quotes?
faqs.a: Getting multiple quotes is normal consumer guidance. The important part is giving each contractor a sufficiently similar brief so the returned scope can be compared fairly.

roof-parts.title: Roof parts explained: ridge, hip, valley, barge, eaves and more
roof-parts.description: Learn the common NZ roof parts and roofing terms, where they sit, what they do and which measurements matter when reading a quote or roof plan.
roof-parts.answer: A roof is easier to understand when you separate the covering from the lines, edges, drainage and penetrations. In NZ roofing language, ridges and hips cover high junctions, valleys collect water between roof planes, barges or verges finish sloping edges, eaves are the lower edges, and flashings weatherproof junctions and penetrations.

sections.title: The roof terms that matter most

blocks.caption: Common roof parts in New Zealand

cells: Ridge
The high, usually horizontal line where two roof planes meet.
Needs a ridge flashing or capping and contributes lineal flashing quantity.
Hip
An external sloping junction where roof planes meet.
Usually receives hip flashing/capping and creates angled cuts in roof sheets or tiles.
Valley
An internal junction between roof planes that collects and carries water.
It is part of the drainage path, so capacity, support and detailing matter.
Barge / verge
The sloping edge at the side of a roof. NZ documents use both terms around the edge and its flashing.
Barge/verge flashing length is separate from roof area.
Eaves
The lower roof edge where water leaves the roof, often into external guttering/spouting.
Eaves length affects drainage, fascia/spouting and some flashing details.
Fascia
A vertical board at the lower ends of rafters or trusses, commonly carrying external spouting/guttering.
It sits at the eaves edge and can be a separate repair/replacement scope from the roof cladding.
Soffit
The enclosed underside of an exterior eave overhang.
It is below the roof edge rather than part of the roof covering, but staining or damage here can point to drainage or moisture issues.
Purlin
A horizontal secondary structural member that supports roof cladding.
Purlin condition and spacing can affect fixing and reroof scope; it is not the same thing as a roofing sheet.
Rafter
A sloping primary structural member running from ridge toward eave and supporting secondary members and roof cladding.
Rafters are framing; roof-covering quotes should not silently assume structural repairs are included.
Apron flashing
Flashing where a roof meets a wall or another upstand.
It protects a change in plane that roof cladding alone cannot weatherproof.
Penetration
An opening through the roof for items such as pipes, ducts, chimneys or roof lights.
Each penetration needs its own compatible weathering detail.

blocks.text: A barge/verge is an edge; a barge flashing is the metal weathering detail at that edge. Likewise, a valley describes the roof junction and can also refer to the drainage component installed there.

sections.title: Which roof lines change quantities and difficulty?

blocks.text: Two roofs with the same square metres can have very different lineal quantities. A simple gable has a ridge and two sloping verge edges; a hip roof adds hips; intersecting roof sections add valleys. Those extra junctions create more flashing, cutting, detailing and opportunities for water to be concentrated.

items: Keep roof area in square metres separate from ridge, hip, valley and barge lengths in metres.
Record penetrations individually rather than hiding them inside a generic complexity percentage.
When comparing quotes, check whether the named flashings and junctions are included, not merely the roofing sheets.
If a term on a plan or quote is unclear, ask what physical roof junction it describes.

sections.title: What is part of roof drainage?

blocks.text: NZMRM uses “gutter” as a broad term for channels that collect and carry roof water, while “spouting” refers specifically to an external gutter. Valleys, internal gutters, secret gutters and roof gutters around obstructions can all be part of the drainage system.

That distinction matters because an external spouting replacement is not the same scope as an internal gutter or valley replacement. Internal drainage elements are more integrated with the building envelope and should be identified clearly in drawings and quotes.

blocks.title: Need drainage rather than terminology?
blocks.text: RoofHub has a separate guide on gutter, spouting and downpipe capacity and quote scope.
blocks.label: Open gutters and downpipes

sections.title: How should these terms appear in a roofing quote?

items: Roof covering/profile and coating named separately.
Ridge, hip, valley and barge/verge scope stated where relevant.
Wall junctions and apron flashings identified.
Penetrations such as flues, pipes, skylights or vents listed rather than assumed.
Gutters/spouting and downpipes clearly included or excluded.
Repairs to fascia, purlins, substrate or framing separated from the cladding scope.

blocks.text: A quote does not need to read like an engineering drawing, but it should be clear enough that two people can tell whether they are pricing the same roof system and the same junctions.

faqs.q: Is a barge the same as a verge?
faqs.a: In everyday NZ roofing usage they refer to the sloping roof edge, while specific documents may use “barge” for the flashing or assembly at that edge and “verge” for the edge itself. Check the drawing or quote context rather than assuming the word alone defines the component.

faqs.q: Is a valley a flashing or a gutter?
faqs.a: It is an internal roof junction that carries water. NZMRM drainage terminology treats valleys as roof-drainage channels, and the installed valley detail also performs a flashing/weathertightness function.

faqs.q: Do hips and valleys change roof area?
faqs.a: They describe the geometry and junctions of roof planes. They may correlate with a more complex shape, but their lineal lengths should not simply be converted into an arbitrary area multiplier.

reroof-process.title: Reroofing process NZ: what happens before, during and after a roof replacement
reroof-process.description: A step-by-step New Zealand reroof process from inspection and scope through safety, removal, substrate checks, new roofing, documentation and final handover.
reroof-process.answer: A good reroof starts before old roofing is removed. The usual sequence is to define the roof condition and specification, confirm consent/LBP and access requirements, agree the written scope and weather plan, remove the old system in controlled stages, inspect what was hidden, install underlay/cladding/flashings and drainage details, then complete clean-up, warranties and required documentation.
