sections.title: 1. Before anyone removes the old roof

items: Identify the existing roofing and any asbestos or hazardous-material uncertainty.
Confirm whether the work is repair, like-for-like replacement, an alteration, or a change of roof system.
Check building-consent and restricted-building-work requirements for the actual project.
Agree the roof product/profile, coating, flashings, drainage, penetrations and any known repairs.
Agree access, scaffold/edge protection, site protection, material storage and waste removal.
Put price, exclusions, allowances, timing, payment and variation rules in writing.

blocks.text: RANZ describes reroofing as a project involving material, system, scope and workmanship decisions. MBIE separately requires all building work to comply with the Building Code even where a consent exemption applies.

sections.title: 2. Plan how the building stays dry and safe

blocks.text: Removing roof cladding temporarily reduces the building’s weather protection. The contractor should plan staging around the forecast, the amount of roof opened at once, temporary protection and how unexpected rain will be handled. The exact method depends on the building and roofing system.

Roof work is also work at height. WorkSafe guidance expects a work plan covering safe access, roof condition, fall hazards, brittle roofing, weather and appropriate controls. Major roof work normally needs purpose-designed access and edge/fall protection rather than treating a ladder as the work platform.

sections.title: 3. Remove the old system and inspect what was hidden

blocks.text: Once old cladding, tiles or membrane are lifted, previously hidden substrate, purlins/battens, framing, underlay and fixings can be assessed. This is the point where a quote allowance for unknown repairs may turn into an actual variation.
A reroof quote should state how unforeseen timber/substrate repairs are authorised and priced. “We will tell you if we find something” is not as useful as a written variation process.

sections.title: 4. Rebuild the roof as a system

blocks.text: The replacement is more than roof sheets. Depending on the system it can involve underlay, battens or purlin interfaces, cladding, fasteners, ridges, hips, valleys, barges, aprons, penetrations and drainage components. Manufacturer instructions and applicable NZ detailing govern the actual installation.
If the roofing has been removed from an inaccessible skillion or low roof, it can also be an important opportunity to assess insulation before the cavity is closed again.

sections.title: 5. Finish with records, warranties and maintenance information

items: Confirm all agreed roof, flashing, penetration and drainage work is complete.
Photograph or record any hidden repairs if useful to the owner.
Collect product and workmanship warranty documents.
Collect maintenance requirements and product identification.
For consented/restricted building work, collect the required records and completion documentation.
Keep the final contract, quote, variations and invoices together.

blocks.text: MBIE consumer-protection guidance requires contractors to provide certain post-build information such as maintenance requirements, guarantees or warranties and applicable insurance documents, regardless of project size.

sections.title: How long does the process take?

blocks.text: The on-roof replacement period and the total project lead time are different. Weather, scaffold, material lead times, complex flashings, hidden repairs, inspections and consent can all change the programme. RoofHub keeps its separate reroof-time guide focused on that question.

blocks.title: Looking for timing rather than sequence?
blocks.text: See the separate RoofHub guide on what changes a reroof programme.
blocks.label: How long does a reroof take?

faqs.q: Do roofers remove the whole old roof at once?
faqs.a: The safe and weather-resilient staging depends on the roof, crew, forecast and temporary-protection plan. A homeowner should understand how much will be opened and how the building will be protected if conditions change.

faqs.q: What happens if rotten timber is found during a reroof?
faqs.a: Hidden repairs should be assessed and agreed through the contract or variation process. The quote should distinguish known scope from provisional or unknown repairs rather than silently adding them later.

faqs.q: What documents should I get after a reroof?
faqs.a: At minimum, collect the final written scope/variations, invoices, product and workmanship warranty information and maintenance requirements. Consented or restricted work may also require council/LBP records.

roofing-contracts.title: Roofing contracts NZ: deposits, payments and variations explained
roofing-contracts.description: Understand NZ roofing contracts, the $30,000 residential building-work threshold, deposits, payment schedules, variations, quotes versus estimates and records to keep.
roofing-contracts.answer: For residential building work costing $30,000 or more including GST, a written contract is mandatory. Below that threshold, a written contract is still sensible. The useful roofing contract is not just a price: it identifies the work, products, start/completion expectations, payment process, defects, dispute process and how variations are agreed before extra work proceeds.

sections.title: When is a written building contract mandatory?

blocks.text: MBIE says a written contract is mandatory when a homeowner contracts directly for residential building work costing $30,000 or more including GST. At that threshold, or if the homeowner asks, the contractor must also provide the prescribed consumer checklist and disclosure statement before signing.
The $30,000 threshold is not a target for splitting work into smaller contracts. MBIE expressly warns contractors not to split work to avoid the consumer-protection requirements.

sections.title: What should a roofing contract actually say?

items: Who the contracting parties are and the project address.
Expected start/completion dates and how delays are handled.
Price or the method used to calculate it.
The roofing work, products/materials and known inclusions.
Who handles any required consents or approvals.
Who carries out and supervises the work.
Payment stages and invoice process.
How defects are remedied.
How disputes are handled.
How variations are agreed before changed work continues.

blocks.text: These are not RoofHub-invented clauses: they reflect the minimum-content themes in MBIE residential building-contract guidance. A particular project may need legal advice or additional terms.

sections.title: How much deposit should you pay a roofer?

blocks.text: Consumer Protection states there is no legal requirement to pay a deposit merely because you accept a quote. If a deposit is requested, its published consumer guidance says not to pay more than 10% of the total cost. The rest of the payment structure should still make sense against materials supplied and work completed.

A project may have legitimate reasons for staged payments or material commitments. The important point is to put the payment schedule in the contract and understand what each payment corresponds to rather than paying an unexplained large amount in advance.

sections.title: Can a roofing quote change?

blocks.caption: Quote, estimate and variation

cells: Fixed quote
Consumer Protection says the provider should complete the agreed work for the quoted price unless you agree to a variation.
Estimate
A best estimate is not the same as a fixed quote; significant changes should be explained and not deliberately understated.
Variation
A change to contracted work. Put scope, price and timing consequences in writing before the changed work proceeds where practicable.

blocks.text: Hidden roof damage is a common reason for legitimate additional work, but “unknown until opening up” should be identified in the original scope and then handled through a documented variation rather than retrospectively blurred into the original quote.

sections.title: What should progress payments be tied to?

blocks.text: MBIE guidance says contracts should describe the payment process and can set out the number, amount and due date of payments. If the contract does not provide a payment schedule, statutory default provisions may apply.

items: Match stages to identifiable work or supplied materials.
Keep invoices and payment records.
Do not assume the final payment means warranty or completion documents no longer matter.
If there is a payment dispute, follow the contract and Construction Contracts Act process rather than improvising.

sections.title: Before signing a roofing contract

items: Compare the final written scope against the quote you accepted.
Check product/profile/coating and major flashings rather than only a brand name.
Confirm removal, scaffold/access, underlay, disposal, drainage and known repairs.
Read the payment and variation clauses.
Check who is responsible for consent and LBP documentation if relevant.
Save the disclosure statement, contract and any later written variations.

faqs.q: Do I legally need a written contract for a $25,000 reroof?
faqs.a: The statutory written-contract threshold is $30,000 or more including GST for residential building work contracted directly with a homeowner. MBIE recommends written contracts below that threshold as well.

faqs.q: Can a roofer ask for more money than the quote?
faqs.a: A fixed quote should cover the agreed work unless you agree to a variation. Legitimate changed or additional work should be identified and agreed rather than simply added without explanation.

faqs.q: Is a 50% roofing deposit normal in New Zealand?
faqs.a: RoofHub does not treat a large deposit as automatically fraudulent, but Consumer Protection says there is no legal requirement to pay a deposit on accepting a quote and advises not paying more than 10% of the total cost if one is requested.

roof-penetrations.title: Roof penetrations NZ: skylights, flues, pipes and vents without creating leak points
roof-penetrations.description: Understand how skylights, flues, pipes, ducts, vents and other roof penetrations should be planned, flashed and included in a New Zealand roofing scope.
roof-penetrations.answer: Every opening through a roof interrupts the cladding and drainage path. NZMRM says the right penetration detail depends on the opening size and shape, roof pitch and type, catchment area and position. Good work treats the penetration as a designed roof junction with compatible flashing and drainage-not as a hole fixed later with sealant.

sections.title: What counts as a roof penetration?

blocks.text: NZMRM defines a penetration as a hole through roof or wall cladding for projections such as pipes, ducts, chimneys and roof lights. On residential roofs that can also include plumbing vents, extractor ducts, solar service routes and other equipment supports.

items: Skylights and roof lights.
Wood-burner or gas flues and chimneys.
Plumbing vent pipes.
Bathroom/kitchen extract ducts where they discharge through the roof.
HVAC and mechanical-service penetrations.
Aerial, cable or solar-related roof interfaces where they penetrate or fix through the cladding.

sections.title: Why position and catchment area matter

blocks.text: A penetration near the ridge sees different water flow from the same opening near the eaves. A wide obstruction can concentrate runoff from the roof above it. NZMRM therefore includes position, roof pitch, roof type and catchment area in the penetration-design decision.
This is why “one pipe boot” is not enough information to price every penetration. A small pipe in one roof pan and a wide skylight crossing several ribs are different roof details.

sections.title: Boot flashing or sheet-metal flashing?

blocks.text: NZMRM groups penetration weathering broadly into proprietary boot flashings and sheet-metal flashings. The suitable option depends on the penetration and roof. The detail needs to accommodate movement, preserve drainage and remain compatible with the roof material.

For metal roofing, compatibility matters above and around the opening. NZMRM says condensate or corrosive discharge from sources such as air-conditioning or solar equipment should not discharge directly onto metal roof cladding but be separately drained to an inert gutter or downpipe.

sections.title: Why sealant alone is not a roof detail

blocks.text: Sealant can be part of a correctly designed junction, but it should not be treated as the whole drainage strategy. The roof still needs laps, upstands, flashings and water paths appropriate to the particular cladding and opening.

items: Ask what flashing system is being used.
Ask whether the penetration crosses one pan or multiple ribs/seams.
Confirm how water from above the penetration bypasses it.
Check material compatibility and movement.
Record the penetration separately in a reroof quote rather than assuming “all flashings” includes it.

sections.title: What happens to existing skylights and flues during a reroof?

blocks.text: A reroof is the time to decide whether an existing penetration is staying, being replaced or being removed. Reusing an old skylight, curb, boot or flue interface can create warranty and compatibility questions even if the surrounding roof is new.

The quote should name significant penetrations and state whether replacement units, new flashing kits, curb work or interior finishing are included. If the condition is unknown until opening, use an allowance or written variation process.

faqs.q: Can a roofer just silicone around a leaking pipe?
faqs.a: A sealant-only repair may not address the underlying drainage, movement or flashing problem. The correct response depends on the penetration and roof detail, and should preserve a durable water path rather than rely solely on surface sealant.

faqs.q: Should I replace an old skylight when I reroof?
faqs.a: Not automatically, but the reroof is a sensible time to assess its age, condition, flashing system, compatibility and warranty. The quote should say whether the existing unit and curb are being reused or replaced.

faqs.q: Does a flue need special metal around it?
faqs.a: Flues are roof penetrations and need a compatible weathering detail suited to their size, temperature, movement, roof profile and position. The exact system should follow the relevant product, roofing and fire/flue requirements.

roof-painting.title: Roof painting or replacement? When coating helps and when it does not
roof-painting.description: A neutral NZ guide to when roof coating/restoration may extend a suitable roof, when defects must be repaired first, and when replacement is the more credible pathway.
roof-painting.answer: Roof painting is maintenance, not a new roof. RANZ’s coating code says coating is not weatherproofing and only extends the life of a suitable existing roof for a limited time. Painting makes sense when the substrate is sound and the problem is mainly the protective surface; perforated corrosion, brittle roofing, failed flashings or widespread substrate failure need repair or replacement first.

sections.title: What roof coating can and cannot do

blocks.text: RANZ’s Roof Coating Code of Practice describes coating as a process that can restore appearance and protect a suitable substrate from degradation, but explicitly says roof coating is not weatherproofing and should not be expected to perform like a new roof.
A fresh colour can make a roof look new from the street. That is not evidence that the roof sheets, tiles, flashings, fixings, underlay or substrate are new or structurally sound.

sections.title: What restoration contractors report  -  and how RoofHub treats that evidence

blocks.title: Restoration is a pathway only when the roof remains a suitable substrate
blocks.synthesis: Commercial restoration businesses consistently describe inspection and defect repair as prerequisites rather than treating paint as a cure-all. RoofHub treats that as useful field evidence, then checks it against RANZ/MRM guidance: coating can be reasonable on a suitable serviceable roof but should not be used to hide perforation, failed details or a roof beyond useful repair.

sections.title: Signs the roof may be a coating candidate

items: The roofing material itself is still sound.
Coating fade, chalking or light surface deterioration is the main problem.
Localised corrosion can be prepared and repaired without widespread perforation.
Flashings and fixings can be repaired to a sound condition before coating.
The coating manufacturer has a preparation/primer/topcoat system suitable for the substrate.

blocks.text: For metal roofs, NZMRM says repaint performance depends on correct surface preparation and compatible coating products. It provides separate preparation guidance for white corrosion, red corrosion, unpainted and pre-painted cladding.

sections.title: Signs painting may be the wrong investment

items: Rust has perforated multiple roof sheets or widespread laps/edges.
Roofing is brittle or no longer safe to load.
Leaks come from failed junctions or material failure that coating will not correct.
The roof needs extensive sheet/tile/flashing replacement before it can even be coated.
Older Decramastic/stone-chip roofing has uncertain asbestos content and would be disturbed by the proposed preparation method.

blocks.text: RANZ says the coating contractor should assess age, condition, extent/cost of repair and practical suitability before accepting a roof for recoating. At some point replacement is the more appropriate option.

sections.title: Will painting stop a leaking roof?

blocks.text: Do not use paint as the diagnosis. A leak caused by a failed penetration, valley, flashing, loose fixing, split sheet or deteriorated membrane needs that defect corrected. Coating may be part of later maintenance, but the water-entry path should be addressed first.

blocks.title: Not sure whether the moisture is a leak?
blocks.text: Use the RoofHub leak-versus-condensation guide before assuming the visible stain identifies the cause.
blocks.label: Check leak vs condensation

sections.title: Roof cleaning and coating is work at height

blocks.text: WorkSafe treats roof washing, moss/lichen treatment, inspection, leak repair and coating as roof-restoration or maintenance work. Appropriate fall controls still apply even where the task is short.
Do not high-pressure spray a roof that may contain asbestos. WorkSafe’s August 2026 warning specifically included a 1970s Decramastic roof that tested positive for chrysotile asbestos.

sections.title: What should a roof-painting quote identify?

items: Roof material and existing coating condition.
Repairs required before coating.
Cleaning/treatment method and asbestos controls where relevant.
Primer and topcoat system, including manufacturer.
Number of coats or specified dry-film system where applicable.
Access/fall-protection scope.
What happens if preparation reveals material too deteriorated to coat.
Product/applicator warranty and maintenance requirements.

faqs.q: Does roof paint make an old roof waterproof again?
faqs.a: No. RANZ describes coating as protective/aesthetic maintenance rather than weatherproofing. Active defects and failed roofing components need repair or replacement.

faqs.q: Can a rusty iron roof be painted?
faqs.a: Light or localised corrosion may be treatable with correct preparation and compatible primers, but perforated or widespread failed steel is a repair/replacement problem rather than something paint can rebuild.

faqs.q: Can you waterblast Decramastic before painting it?
faqs.a: Not until asbestos risk is resolved. WorkSafe says high-pressure water and compressed air must not be used on asbestos-containing material, and its 2026 warning included a 1970s Decramastic roof that tested positive for chrysotile asbestos.

roof-ventilation.title: Roof ventilation NZ: when it helps condensation and when it is not the whole answer
roof-ventilation.description: Understand NZ roof-space ventilation, condensation, cold and warm roofs, moisture sources, airtight ceilings and why adding vents is not a universal fix.
roof-ventilation.answer: Roof ventilation is mainly a moisture-management tool, not a cure-all. BRANZ says roof-space moisture can come from inside the house as well as outside, and well-managed indoor humidity plus an airtight ceiling remain important. Ventilation can help some roof assemblies, but its design needs to suit the roof, climate and moisture path rather than simply adding the maximum number of vents.

sections.title: What roof-space ventilation is trying to do

blocks.text: BRANZ describes the purpose of roof-space ventilation in New Zealand as primarily moisture management above ceiling insulation and below roof cladding, helping keep moisture-sensitive building elements dry enough to perform and remain durable.
NZMRM treats ventilation pathways as part of the roof assembly and internal-moisture strategy rather than an isolated accessory.

sections.title: Start with where the moisture is coming from

blocks.text: BRANZ notes that roof-space moisture can come from occupant activities and air leakage from living spaces. If warm moist indoor air is continually entering a cold roof cavity, adding vents without improving the moisture source or ceiling air leakage may not solve the underlying problem.

items: Check bathroom/kitchen extraction actually discharges outdoors.
Check obvious ceiling penetrations and access hatches for uncontrolled air leakage where relevant.
Confirm insulation is not wet, displaced or blocking designed ventilation paths.
Inspect underlay, roof leaks and drainage defects separately.
Treat ventilation as one part of the diagnosis, not a substitute for finding the moisture source.

sections.title: Is more ventilation always better?

blocks.text: No. BRANZ has documented that roof ventilation is context-dependent and that even excessive ventilation can worsen condensation in particular designs and climates. The roof assembly, indoor moisture, outside conditions and air pathway all matter.

Avoid rules such as “every metal roof needs X vents” without checking the roof design and the ventilation system being proposed. Product and design guidance should define intake, exhaust and weathering details.

sections.title: Roof-cavity ventilation is not the same as ventilating the home

blocks.text: A system that exchanges air within or through the roof cavity is a different question from a home ventilation system supplying habitable rooms. Building Performance warns against deliberately supplying contaminated roof-space air into the house, particularly where asbestos-containing roofing may be present.
For living-space ventilation, fresh outside air and source extraction are separate design decisions. Do not assume a roof cavity is automatically a clean air source.

sections.title: Why reroofing is a useful time to review ventilation

blocks.text: A reroof can expose underlay, insulation interfaces and previously inaccessible roof-space details. If there has been recurring condensation, mould or wet insulation, define the moisture-management plan before the new cladding closes the assembly.

blocks.title: Seeing water already?
blocks.text: First separate likely rainwater ingress from roof-space condensation.
blocks.label: Leak or condensation?

faqs.q: Do all New Zealand roofs need added vents?
faqs.a: No universal rule fits every roof. BRANZ treats ventilation as one moisture-control strategy whose need and design depend on the roof assembly, climate, indoor moisture and air leakage.

faqs.q: Will a whirlybird stop roof condensation?
faqs.a: It may increase air movement in some roofs, but it will not correct every moisture source or assembly problem. The diagnosis should include indoor moisture, ceiling air leakage, insulation, underlay and the intended intake/exhaust path.

faqs.q: Can I use air from the roof space to ventilate the house?
faqs.a: Roof-space air can contain dust, mould, vermin contamination or hazardous particles. A living-space ventilation design should follow current Building Performance guidance and should not assume the roof cavity is a safe fresh-air source.

roof-problems.title: Common roof problems NZ: what the symptom may mean and what to check next
roof-problems.description: Use common roof symptoms such as stains, rust, overflowing gutters, lifting sheets, mould and cracked tiles to identify the next inspection step without pretending a symptom is a diagnosis.
roof-problems.answer: A roof symptom is a clue, not a diagnosis. Water marks can come from rain entry or condensation; rust can be cosmetic or structural; overflowing spouting can be blockage or undersizing. Start by recording when and where the symptom occurs, then inspect the relevant roof line, flashing, penetration, drainage or roof-space condition before deciding on repair or replacement.

blocks.caption: Roof symptom triage

cells: Ceiling stain after wind-driven rain

sections.title: What information makes a roof problem easier to diagnose?

items: When it occurs: only heavy rain, wind-driven rain, winter mornings, all the time.
Exact indoor location and whether it moves or spreads.
Roof material and approximate age if known.
Nearby roof features: valley, chimney, skylight, wall junction, solar panel or gutter.
Photos from the ground and inside the roof space where safe.
Any recent roofing, solar, aerial, HVAC or cleaning work.
Whether the issue is isolated or repeated in several areas.

blocks.text: This context helps separate a roofing defect from condensation, plumbing or another source. It also gives a roofer something more useful than “the roof leaks somewhere”.

sections.title: When should you treat it as urgent?

items: Active water entry near electrical fittings.
Loose roofing or debris after a storm.
Sagging, visibly unstable or severely corroded roofing.
A suspected asbestos roof that has been broken, drilled or high-pressure cleaned.
Overflow from internal gutters or drainage that can enter the building.
Any situation that would require an untrained person to climb onto an unsafe roof to investigate.

blocks.text: Work from the ground where possible. WorkSafe treats roof inspection and maintenance as work-at-height hazards and identifies severely corroded metal, some old tiles, glass/skylights and fibrolite as examples of brittle roofing.

sections.title: Does a problem mean repair or replacement?

blocks.text: Not by itself. A local failed flashing or isolated sheet can be a repair; repeated failures, widespread corrosion, brittle roofing or a roof system at the end of its practical service life can make replacement more sensible. The condition and extent matter more than the drama of a single symptom.

blocks.title: Need the decision framework?
blocks.text: RoofHub separates repairable local defects from broader system-failure signs.
blocks.label: Repair or replace?

faqs.q: Why is my roof leaking only when it is windy?
faqs.a: Wind-driven rain can expose junctions that do not leak in vertical rain, including flashings, penetrations and laps. The entry point can also be upslope or sideways from the visible ceiling stain.

faqs.q: Does rust mean I need a new metal roof?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Surface corrosion can sometimes be prepared and protected, while perforation or widespread loss of substrate is a different problem. The extent and location of corrosion matter.

faqs.q: Why does my gutter overflow only in very heavy rain?
faqs.a: Possible causes include blockage, outlet/downpipe constraints, poor fall or a system that is undersized for the catchment and design rainfall. Roof drainage should be checked as a system rather than by guessing from one component.

solar-roof.title: Solar panels and roofing NZ: what to check before installing or reroofing
solar-roof.description: Plan roof-mounted solar around roof condition, remaining roof life, structural fixings, wind, weathertightness, penetrations, warranties and the 2025 NZ building-consent exemptions.
solar-roof.answer: Solar panels and roofing should be planned together. Since 23 October 2025, qualifying roof-mounted solar arrays can use new building-consent exemptions, but the Building Code, local planning rules and exemption conditions still apply. Before installing panels, check the roof’s remaining life, fixing method, wind conditions and weathertightness so you do not create an expensive remove-and-refit problem when the roof soon needs replacement.

sections.title: What changed for roof-mounted solar consent in 2025?

blocks.text: Building Performance says new Schedule 1 exemptions for roof-mounted solar took effect on 23 October 2025. Arrays under 40 m² in wind conditions no greater than high have one exemption pathway; arrays over 40 m² or in higher wind require structural fixing design or review by a Chartered Professional Engineer to use the exemption.
“Exempt from building consent” does not mean “no rules”. The installation still needs to comply with the Building Code, local district-plan requirements and the detailed exemption conditions.

sections.title: Should you reroof before installing solar?

blocks.text: If the roof is likely to need replacement during the solar system’s useful life, coordinate the projects before installation. Removing and reinstalling arrays later adds labour and creates another round of roof interfaces. The decision should consider roof condition, corrosion, existing leaks, coating life and major flashings rather than roof age alone.

items: Ask for a roof-condition inspection before solar if the roof is older or already showing problems.
Record the exact mounting system and attachment points.
Keep product and workmanship warranties for both roof and solar systems.
Ask who is responsible if roofing must be removed under the array later.

sections.title: Fixings and penetrations are roof details, not just solar hardware

blocks.text: Any roof fixing must preserve structure and weathertightness. Where a solar installation creates penetrations or service routes, the roof detail should follow the relevant roofing/product system rather than relying on improvised sealant.
NZMRM also warns that condensate or discharge associated with services should not be directed onto metal roof cladding where it can create a corrosive local environment.

sections.title: Questions to ask the solar installer and roofer

items: What roof material/profile is present and what mounting system is compatible with it?
Does the array size/wind condition fit the consent exemption, and is engineering required?
Does the system penetrate the cladding or use profile/seam-specific clamps?
Who warrants the roof interface and for how long?
How are cables and services routed without creating water traps?
What happens to the panels if the roof needs repainting, repair or replacement?
Will the roof manufacturer/installer warranty be affected by third-party fixings?

faqs.q: Do roof-mounted solar panels need building consent in NZ?
faqs.a: Many can now use Schedule 1 exemptions. The detailed pathway depends on array size and design wind speed; larger arrays or higher-wind sites require structural fixing design/review by a Chartered Professional Engineer to use the exemption.

faqs.q: Should I replace an old roof before getting solar?
faqs.a: If the roof is approaching repair/replacement or already has corrosion, leaks or coating failure, coordinating the reroof first can avoid paying to remove and reinstall the solar system later. Assess condition rather than age alone.

faqs.q: Can solar installers just drill through metal roofing?
faqs.a: The fixing method must preserve structure and weathertightness and be compatible with the roof profile and materials. Any penetration needs a designed weathering detail, not simply a hole plus sealant.

roof-insulation-reroof.title: Roof insulation when reroofing NZ: when the open roof creates an opportunity
roof-insulation-reroof.description: Understand when reroofing is a useful or required opportunity to improve ceiling/skillion-roof insulation, and why moisture, clearances and rental rules matter.
roof-insulation-reroof.answer: Reroofing does not automatically mean every house must be upgraded to the newest roof-insulation specification, but opening an inaccessible roof can create a valuable opportunity-and for some rental properties, an obligation-to install or upgrade insulation that could not previously be accessed. Plan insulation, underlay, clearances and moisture management together before the new roofing closes the cavity.

sections.title: Why a reroof can be the best time to insulate

blocks.text: Building Performance says ceilings without accessible roof spaces can be difficult to retrofit, and replacing the roofing or ceiling lining can be a good opportunity because the cavity becomes accessible. This is particularly relevant to skillion and very low-pitch roofs.

Tenancy Services similarly identifies inaccessible skillion/low roof spaces and says landlords must install insulation where an access exception ends because work such as reroofing now makes installation reasonably practicable.

sections.title: Does every reroof have to meet the latest H1 roof R-value?

blocks.text: Do not assume a simple yes/no rule from a new-build R-value table. MBIE has specific guidance for repairs, replacements and alterations to existing buildings under H1. The requirement depends on the nature of the work and building, while separate Healthy Homes rules apply to rental properties.

For a real project, separate three questions: what the Building Code requires for the building work, what rental Healthy Homes standards require if applicable, and what energy-performance upgrade the owner chooses voluntarily.

sections.title: Insulation must be coordinated with moisture control

blocks.text: Adding insulation changes temperatures and available air space within the roof assembly. Building Performance warns that poor installation can create moisture problems and notes clearances between insulation and underlay can be required depending on the construction.
If the roof already has condensation, wet insulation or mould, resolve the moisture pathway rather than simply packing more insulation into the cavity.

sections.title: What to put in the reroof scope

items: Existing insulation type, condition and approximate coverage.
Whether the cavity becomes accessible only after cladding removal.
Target insulation approach and who installs it.
Required clearances around electrical fittings, flues and ventilation pathways.
How roof underlay and insulation are separated or supported.
Whether rental-property Healthy Homes obligations apply.
Photos or records before the roof closes if future access will be difficult.

faqs.q: Do I need building consent just to add ceiling insulation?
faqs.a: Building Performance says ceiling and floor insulation retrofits generally do not require building consent, but the surrounding roofing/building work may have its own consent requirements and all work still needs to comply with applicable rules.

faqs.q: If my rental has a skillion roof, do I need to insulate it when reroofing?
faqs.a: Tenancy Services says an inaccessible-roof exception can end when work such as reroofing makes the space accessible; landlords then need to meet the applicable Healthy Homes insulation requirements where insulation is required.

faqs.q: Can insulation touch the roofing underlay?
faqs.a: That depends on the roof assembly and current product/design requirements. Building Performance notes that moisture problems and clearances must be considered, so do not assume the cavity can simply be filled solid.

roof-insurance.title: Roof insurance NZ: storm damage, maintenance and what to document
roof-insurance.description: Understand the common NZ insurance distinction between sudden roof damage and gradual deterioration, what to document after a storm and why policy wording and maintenance matter.
roof-insurance.answer: Home insurance commonly responds differently to sudden accidental storm damage and gradual deterioration such as long-term corrosion or wear. After roof damage, make the property safe without creating further risk, photograph what happened, contact the insurer promptly and keep damaged items until the insurer tells you what can be discarded. Your own policy wording decides cover.

sections.title: Sudden damage and gradual deterioration are different questions

blocks.text: ICNZ explains that house policies are generally designed around sudden, unexpected events, while wear, corrosion, rot and other gradual deterioration are commonly excluded. Resultant interior damage can have different treatment depending on the policy and how the damage occurred.

Do not assume “water got in during a storm” automatically means the deteriorated roof itself is insured. The insurer may distinguish the storm event, the condition of the roof and any resulting interior damage.

sections.title: What to do after storm damage

items: Keep people away from loose roofing, live electrical hazards and unsafe roof areas.
Photograph visible damage from safe locations.
Record the date/time and what weather or event occurred.
Contact the insurer promptly and ask what temporary protection is authorised.
Do not dispose of damaged materials before checking with the insurer where they may need assessment.
Keep emergency repair invoices and contractor reports.

blocks.text: ICNZ says insurers typically need the circumstances, detailed damage information and timing, and may send an assessor. It recommends photographs and checking before disposing of damaged items.

sections.title: Why roof maintenance can affect a claim

blocks.text: ICNZ says reasonable care and maintenance are important because insurance is not intended to replace normal upkeep. A roof already perforated by long-term corrosion is a different risk from sound roofing suddenly damaged by wind.
Keeping maintenance records, photos and invoices can help establish what condition the roof was in before an event, but they do not override the terms, limits or exclusions of the policy.

sections.title: Can you repair the roof before the insurer assesses it?

blocks.text: Safety and preventing further loss come first, but coordinate non-emergency permanent work with the insurer. Ask what temporary measures, contractor reports, photographs and retained materials they need before substantial repairs remove the evidence.
RoofHub cannot determine whether a claim is covered. Policy wording, the cause of damage, maintenance history and the insurer’s assessment control the outcome.

sections.title: If the roof needs full replacement

blocks.text: If an event exposes that the roof was already near end of life, the insurer and owner may separate insured damage from maintenance or betterment. Get the scope in writing and understand who is paying for what before committing to a full reroof.

blocks.title: Need to scope the replacement itself?
blocks.text: Use RoofHub’s reroof process and cost tools separately from the insurance coverage decision.
blocks.label: Open reroof process

faqs.q: Does house insurance cover a rusty leaking roof?
faqs.a: Policies commonly exclude gradual deterioration such as wear, rust or corrosion, although resulting damage can be treated differently depending on the policy and circumstances. Check your insurer’s wording and assessment.

faqs.q: Should I throw away storm-damaged roofing?
faqs.a: Not before checking with the insurer if it may be relevant to the claim. Photograph the damage and ask what the insurer or assessor needs to inspect or retain.

faqs.q: Does insurance pay for a complete reroof after a storm?
faqs.a: It depends on the insured event, pre-existing roof condition, policy wording and whether full replacement is necessary to remedy insured damage. RoofHub cannot determine coverage from the fact that a storm occurred.

rusting-metal-roof.title: Rusting metal roof: repair, restore or replace?
rusting-metal-roof.description: A neutral NZ decision guide for surface corrosion, local rust, perforated sheets, failing fixings and widespread metal-roof deterioration.
rusting-metal-roof.answer: Rust does not automatically mean a full reroof. Surface coating deterioration and small local defects may be repair/restoration candidates; isolated perforated sheets or flashings may sometimes be replaced locally; widespread corrosion, holes across several areas or repeated leaks make a whole-roof replacement comparison more important. The key is how deep and widespread the failure is, not simply whether rust is visible.

blocks.synthesis: The field sources support more than one pathway: local sheet/fixing/flashing work or restoration can be credible when deterioration is limited, while widespread perforation and repeated failures push the decision toward replacement. Manufacturer guidance adds product/environment/maintenance constraints but does not decide whether a particular existing roof is repairable.

sections.title: Why did the corrosion start?

blocks.text: Exposure, areas that do not receive normal rain washing, debris, incompatible details, cut edges, fixings, ponding/poor drainage and coating breakdown can all change corrosion risk. The remedy should address the cause as well as the visible rust.

Do not sand, scrape, waterblast or drill an older unknown roof merely to “see how bad the rust is”. Some historic textured metal tiles and other roofing products can involve asbestos or brittle-roofing risk.

sections.title: Questions that make the repair-vs-reroof decision clearer

items: Is corrosion confined to one detail/sheet or repeated across multiple roof faces?
Is there only coating/surface deterioration, or are there pinholes/perforations/missing metal?
Are leaks present in one area or several unrelated areas?
Have similar repairs already been repeated?
Are flashings, fixings and valleys in comparable condition to the main sheets?
What does the product/environment maintenance guidance require for this location?

sections.title: If you are getting prices

blocks.text: Ask the contractor to separate local repairs, surface preparation/coating, sheet or flashing replacement and full reroof scope. A low repaint price and a higher reroof price are not directly comparable unless the coating proposal establishes that the substrate is actually suitable.

blocks.title: One roofer says paint it and another says reroof?
blocks.text: Start with the repair/restore/replace framework, then compare the written scopes rather than assuming either seller is neutral.
blocks.label: Compare the decision

sections.title: What RoofHub would ask next

blocks.text: The most useful next facts are roof system, whether corrosion is local or widespread, whether the metal is actually perforated, whether leaks recur in different areas, and whether there are safety/asbestos concerns. Those facts are more decision-relevant than roof age alone.

blocks.title: Use the neutral condition framework
blocks.text: Ask RoofHub to work through the condition facts, or use the condition-assessment guide before requesting prices.
blocks.label: Assess the roof condition

faqs.q: Can one rusty roof sheet be replaced without reroofing everything?
faqs.a: Potentially, if the defect is truly local, a compatible repair/replacement is available and the surrounding roof/details remain serviceable. A site check still needs to establish why that sheet failed and whether similar corrosion is present elsewhere.

faqs.q: Will painting stop a rusty roof leaking?
faqs.a: Not if the underlying roof is perforated or defective. RANZ/MRM guidance treats preparation and repair as prerequisites; a coating is not a substitute for failed roofing or flashings.

recurring-roof-leaks.title: Roof keeps leaking after repair: what should be checked next?
recurring-roof-leaks.description: A NZ troubleshooting guide for recurring roof leaks, repeat patching, wind-driven rain, flashings, valleys, penetrations, drainage and condensation.
recurring-roof-leaks.answer: A recurring leak does not automatically mean the whole roof needs replacing, but it does mean the diagnosis should be revisited. Water can enter away from the ceiling stain, one failed detail can be missed, wind direction can change the entry path, and condensation can imitate a leak. Repeated failures in different roof areas are a stronger whole-roof warning than one repair that needs correcting.

sections.title: Treat the return of the leak as a diagnosis problem first

blocks.text: The place water appears inside is not always the point where rain entered. Roof geometry, underlay, framing and gravity can move water before it becomes visible. Repeating the same patch without confirming the entry path can therefore repeat the failure.

blocks.title: A local repair can be enough  -  when the failure really is local
blocks.synthesis: Published practitioner examples show both sides of the decision: some leaks are resolved with targeted flashing/valley work, while repeated failures across multiple areas can indicate a broader roof-system problem. RoofHub therefore treats recurrence pattern and spread as more useful than “it leaked again” by itself.

A side-lap, flashing, penetration or junction exposed from a particular direction.

sections.title: Details worth checking before blaming the whole roof

items: Valleys and valley terminations.
Apron, barge, ridge and junction flashings.
Skylights, flues, pipes, vents and other penetrations.
Fasteners, laps and local sheet/tile damage.
Gutters, internal gutters, outlets and overflow paths.
Condensation, wet insulation and roof-space moisture where rain correlation is weak.

sections.title: When does a recurring leak justify a replacement comparison?

blocks.text: A whole-roof replacement comparison becomes more useful when failures are appearing in unrelated areas, corrosion/material breakdown is widespread, multiple details are nearing end of useful repair, or opening-up shows broader substrate/system problems. It is not justified simply because one contractor repair needs revisiting.

sections.title: What to record for the roofer

items: Date/time and whether it was actively raining.
Wind direction or whether the leak appears only in driven rain, if known.
Which room/ceiling area became wet.
Photos from indoors or ground level  -  never by climbing onto the roof.
Previous repair location and what was reportedly changed.
Whether other roof areas have started leaking too.

faqs.q: Does the ceiling stain show exactly where the roof is leaking?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Water can travel along roof components or framing before it appears internally, so the entry point should be traced rather than inferred from the stain alone.

faqs.q: If the same leak came back, should I replace the whole roof?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Revisit the diagnosis and repair scope first. Replacement becomes more plausible when there is broader deterioration or repeated failure in different roof areas.

concrete-tile-decision.title: Concrete tile roof: repair, restore or replace?
concrete-tile-decision.description: A neutral NZ guide to cracked tiles, ridge/hip pointing, coating/restoration, underlay and when a concrete tile roof may need replacement.
concrete-tile-decision.answer: Concrete tile roofs do not automatically need replacement because a few tiles are cracked or the coating looks tired. Local tile/pointing repairs can be appropriate for isolated defects, and a suitable roof can sometimes be restored after repairs. Replacement becomes more credible when the roof material or supporting system is beyond useful repair, defects are widespread, underlay/detailing problems are significant, or the cost of making the old roof reliable becomes disproportionate.

blocks.title: Repair and restoration examples from NZ tile-roof practitioners

sections.title: Do not judge the roof only by tile colour

blocks.text: Visible fading or surface weathering is different from cracked/slipped tiles, failed ridge/hip work, damaged valleys/flashings, underlay issues or supporting-system problems. A coating decision should follow a condition assessment and repairs, not replace them.
RoofHub does not assume that a concrete tile roof “needs painting to be waterproof”. Coating and restoration claims are kept separate from the condition of the roof system and the actual leak path.

sections.title: Useful questions before accepting a restoration or replacement proposal

items: How many tiles are damaged, and is damage clustered or widespread?
Are ridge/hip bedding and pointing locally defective or failing broadly?
What condition are valleys, flashings and penetrations in?
Is the underlay accessible/known, and are there signs of repeated moisture entry?
Are replacement tiles compatible and available?
What exact defects will coating/restoration fix  -  and what will it not fix?
If replacement is proposed, is it like-for-like tile or a conversion to another roof system, and what structural/detail changes follow?

blocks.text: Changing roof system is a separate design/scope decision from deciding whether the existing roof is repairable. Weight, battens/purlins, flashings, geometry, insulation/underlay and consent/RBW context may all need review.

faqs.q: Do a few cracked concrete tiles mean the roof needs replacing?
faqs.a: No. BRANZ specifically publishes repair guidance for isolated clay/concrete tile concerns. Whether local repair is enough depends on the wider tile, pointing, underlay and flashing condition.

faqs.q: Is painting a concrete tile roof the same as fixing it?
faqs.a: No. Restoration can include repairs and coating, but the coating itself is not a substitute for damaged tiles, failed details or an unsuitable roof system.

faqs.q: Can I pressure-wash an old Decramastic roof to see its condition?
faqs.a: Do not do that while asbestos content is uncertain. WorkSafe has specifically warned about high-pressure spraying of asbestos-containing roofing. Identify/manage the material safely first.

faqs.q: Does every Decramastic roof need replacing?
faqs.a: No universal rule follows from the name alone. Safe material identification plus the actual extent of corrosion, perforation, leaks and system condition should determine whether local work or reroofing is credible.

hidden-reroof-problems.title: Hidden problems found during a reroof: timber, underlay, moisture and variations
hidden-reroof-problems.description: What NZ reroofing can uncover after the old roof comes off, how to plan for hidden timber or substrate work, and how variations should be handled.
hidden-reroof-problems.answer: Some reroof problems cannot be confirmed until the old covering is removed. Purlins/battens, substrate, old underlay, moisture damage and historic detailing can be partly concealed. A good quote should therefore separate known scope from opening-up uncertainty and state how additional work will be assessed, authorised and priced instead of pretending every hidden item is included or zero-cost.

sections.title: What can genuinely be hidden before strip-off?

items: Purlin, batten, deck/substrate or framing deterioration behind the roof covering.
Older or deteriorated underlay that cannot be fully seen beforehand.
Moisture staining/decay around long-running leaks.
Historic flashing/junction work concealed by later roofing or sealant.
Different roof sections or additions built at different times and to different details.
Asbestos or other hazardous-material implications where the existing product is uncertain.

blocks.title: Three NZ contractor accounts of opening-up uncertainty
blocks.synthesis: The value of these contractor sources is not that every reroof will need timber replacement. It is that separate publishers describe concealed conditions becoming visible only after opening the roof. One Mt Eden project’s reported 35 linear metres of purlin replacement is therefore an example of uncertainty, not a quantity allowance RoofHub applies to another house.

sections.title: How the quote should deal with unknown work

blocks.text: The written scope should say what timber/substrate repair is already included, what is excluded or provisional, who can authorise additional work and how a variation is priced. Consumer building-contract rules also matter for qualifying residential building work.

blocks.caption: Useful ways to describe opening-up risk

cells: “Timber repairs extra if required.”
What timber repair is included, what triggers a variation, how will quantity/rate be recorded and who approves it before work proceeds?
“Underlay included.”
Which underlay/system is included, and what happens if the substrate/support beneath it needs repair?
“Make good as required.”
Which components are covered by “make good”, and which are an allowance or excluded?

sections.title: Document what is found before it disappears again

blocks.text: For significant unexpected work, photographs and a short written variation record can make the final invoice, warranty history and future maintenance easier to understand. This is especially useful because the repaired timber/substrate may be hidden again once the new roof is installed.
RoofHub does not use one contractor project as a default timber allowance. Hidden-work quantities are project-specific unless they were measured or specifically included in the quote.

faqs.q: Can a roofer know exactly how much rotten timber is under the old roof before stripping it?
faqs.a: Sometimes some defects are visible or inferable beforehand, but concealed battens/purlins/substrate can remain uncertain until opening-up. The quote should explain how that uncertainty is handled.

faqs.q: Does RoofHub add a standard timber allowance to every reroof?
faqs.a: No. A project-specific contractor case can demonstrate the risk of hidden work, but it is not a defensible universal quantity or price allowance for another roof.

roof-condition-assessment.title: Roof condition assessment: what to check before deciding repair or replacement
roof-condition-assessment.description: A neutral NZ roof-condition framework for homeowners and professionals: what can be checked safely, what photos/aerial imagery can and cannot show, and when site inspection is needed.
roof-condition-assessment.answer: A useful roof-condition assessment separates the roof covering from the details around it, records whether defects are local or widespread, and looks for recurrence, active leaks, drainage, flashings, penetrations, underlay/substrate and safety constraints. Photos and aerial imagery can help describe a roof, but they cannot reliably prove hidden condition or watertightness. RoofHub can help organise the decision; a competent on-site inspection is still needed when the conclusion depends on concealed or close-up condition.

sections.title: The six condition facts that change the decision most

items: Roof system: metal, concrete tile, pressed metal tile, membrane or unknown.
Spread: one local area, several areas, or widespread.
Recurrence: first occurrence, same area repeatedly, or different areas over time.
Visible condition from a safe place: surface wear, local damage, holes/missing material, or sagging/movement.
Leak pattern: none, one area or multiple areas; whether it correlates with rain/wind.
Safety/material constraints: possible asbestos, brittle roofing, unsafe access or structural movement.

blocks.text: Roof age is useful context but is deliberately not one of RoofHub’s hard decision rules. A newer roof can have a local installation/detail failure; an older roof can still contain serviceable areas.

sections.title: What RoofHub can and cannot do remotely

blocks.caption: Remote information is useful when its limits stay explicit

cells: Ground-level or safely obtained photos
Visible profile/material, obvious local damage, roof edges/details, symptom location.
Hidden corrosion, underlay condition, substrate/timber condition or guaranteed leak diagnosis.
Plans or measured drawings
Roof geometry, areas, slopes, roof lines, penetrations and estimating scope.
Current physical condition unless inspection notes/photos accompany them.
Aerial / satellite imagery
Rough geometry, number of roof sections, large penetrations and site/access context.
Reliable corrosion severity, fastener condition, underlay, hidden timber, watertightness or whether a roof needs replacement.
Written repair/inspection reports and contractor photos
What a competent person observed on site and what scope they propose.
Independent proof unless evidence can be checked; contractor commercial interest still matters.

blocks.text: Do not climb onto a roof to provide RoofHub with better photos. Work at height and brittle roofing need proper controls; use safe ground-level/internal photos or material already obtained by a competent person.

sections.title: RoofHub’s neutral triage is deliberately conservative

blocks.text: The Smart Assistant can organise user-supplied facts into five directions: repair plausible, restoration plausible, replacement plausible, inspection needed or safety first. It does not diagnose a roof. It is designed to avoid both “every leak needs a reroof” and “patch everything forever” by asking about spread, recurrence and visible failure before recommending the next step.

blocks.title: Why RoofHub keeps practitioner recommendations separate
blocks.synthesis: Different roofing businesses sell different mixes of repair, restoration and reroofing. That does not make their observations useless; it means RoofHub records the commercial interest and looks for the condition signals underneath the recommendation. The goal is the lowest adequate intervention supported by the facts, with inspection where remote information cannot settle the issue.

sections.title: If photo review is added later, ask for evidence  -  not risky access

items: A full-roof/context photo from the ground where possible.
Close-up photos only if they already exist or can be taken safely without roof access.
Interior ceiling stain/moisture photos and approximate location.
Roof-space photos only where the area is normally safe and accessible; do not enter unsafe/confined spaces for RoofHub.
Any prior roofer inspection photos or repair descriptions.
Approximate roof age/system only as context, not as the deciding rule.

blocks.text: A future photo-assisted workflow can improve triage, but it should preserve the same limits: image interpretation is an observation aid, not a substitute for destructive/opening-up inspection, moisture testing or professional judgement where those are needed.

faqs.q: Can Google Earth tell if my roof needs replacing?
faqs.a: No. Aerial imagery can help with roof shape, sections and context, but it usually cannot reliably establish corrosion depth, fastener/underlay/substrate condition, hidden timber or watertightness.

faqs.q: Can RoofHub tell me repair or replace from photos?
faqs.a: Photos can support a directional triage when they show relevant condition safely, but they do not turn a remote review into an inspection. RoofHub should state what is visible, what remains unknown and when a site inspection is needed.

faqs.q: What is the most important thing to tell RoofHub?
faqs.a: Describe the roof system, whether the problem is local or widespread, whether it is recurring, and what visible condition you can observe safely. Those facts usually change the repair-vs-replace direction more than age alone.
